    Breaking: Intel continues layoffs with cuts to its IT department, hundreds of employees reportedly affected

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (494 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Tomshardware

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Intel has reduced its workforce by approximately 27,800 employees under Lip-Bu Tan, based on the company's reported headcount figures, but this does not seem to be enough.
    • In a recent development, the latest cuts in Intel's IT organization reportedly began on November 16, although Intel has not disclosed how many employees will lose their jobs, notes TrendForce citing CTech.
    • Recent findings suggest that the latest reductions follow several rounds of layoffs throughout 2026.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Intel has reduced its workforce by approximately 27,800 employees under Lip-Bu Tan, based on the company's reported headcount figures, but this does not seem to be enough. The company has reportedly initiated another round of layoffs, this time across its global information technology (IT) organization, as its chief executive continues to reduce expenses and simplify the company's operations, reports Business Insider.

    In a recent development, the latest cuts in Intel's IT organization reportedly began on November 16, although Intel has not disclosed how many employees will lose their jobs, notes TrendForce citing CTech. Some employees claim that the reductions could affect a double-digit percentage of the department's workforce of around 2,607 people at 55 sites in 53 countries, so we are talking about at least 260 people if we are talking about a 10% reduction, or as much as 520 if we are talking about a 20% reduction. One has to keep in mind that these estimates have not been independently verified. Intel has neither confirmed the number of affected employees nor identified the specific teams involved. Instead, the company reiterated to Business Insider that it regularly reviews its workforce to ensure that personnel and financial resources correspond to its strategic priorities.

    Recent findings suggest that the latest reductions follow several rounds of layoffs throughout 2026. In July, Intel eliminated positions in its Data Center and AI Group. Between July and October, the company submitted nine Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification (WARN) notices in California, which covered 222 employees, according to Business Insider. The most recent notice, filed on October 22, concerned 67 permanent job cuts at Intel's Folsom campus (which mostly specializes in R&D, hardware validation, and software development), effective October 31. As of November 17, no additional WARN notices had been reported.

    In a recent development, intel employed 81,100 people as of September 27, 2026, including 76,500 employees at Intel itself and another 4,600 at Mobileye and other subsidiaries. This compares with 85,100 employees at the end of 2025 and 108,900 a year earlier, which means that the company's workforce declined by 4,000 since December, 2025, and 27,800 since December, 2024. respectively.

    Intel's workforce reductions began well before Lip-Bu Tan became chief executive in 2025. In 2024, his predecessor Pat Gelsinger announced plans to eliminate more than 15,000 positions, or approximately 15% of the company’s workforce. Tan has continued to reduce expenses, eliminate management layers, and discontinue lower-priority projects as Intel attempts to cut costs and reduce losses/improve profitability.

    Over in China, though, things have been taken to the next level when it comes to checking on who is actually paying attention to the lessons.

    SCMP noted that the China University of Mining and Technology in Jiangsu tracks the “classroom status” of students. This identified students who checked their phones during class, as well as flagging some as being asleep – even though they had been collecting notes.

    Autonomous 5-ton John Deere skid-steer loader trained to perform acrobatic maneuvers using AI

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that videos of an incredibly acrobatic, nimble, and graceful John Deere 5-ton skid-steer loader have been shared by a group of researchers from the U.S.
    • Researchers have used reinforcement learning to teach a 5-tonne John Deere skid-steer loader to perform complex acrobatic manoeuvres autonomously.
    • If you unfurl the video embed above, you can see a hulking 332G skid-steer do some astonishing tricks.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that videos of an incredibly acrobatic, nimble, and graceful John Deere 5-ton skid-steer loader have been shared by a group of researchers from the U.S. and Switzerland. A recently published paper titled Heavy Metal Acrobatics provides the reasoning behind this eyebrow-raising autonomous robotics feat. It is hoped this research will be useful in the future automation of heavy machinery in industries like construction, mining, and material handling. It also demonstrates that reinforcement learning in a simulation can transfer remarkably well to the real world.

    Researchers have used reinforcement learning to teach a 5-tonne John Deere skid-steer loader to perform complex acrobatic manoeuvres autonomously. Trained in simulation and transferred to a real machine, the system can balance on two wheels, navigate rough terrain, spin, and control its bucket before landing safely. The research demonstrates the potential of AI-driven automation for heavy construction and industrial machinery. Video Credit: @leggedrobotics / @ETH Paper: https://t.co/MT7fyZ54Hk #engineering #technologyNovember 17, 2026.

    If you unfurl the video embed above, you can see a hulking 332G skid-steer do some astonishing tricks. It hops back and forth on two wheels, pirouettes, and balances while flexing its lift arm. Moreover, it does these moves while never looking like it will teeter over. The researchers claim that “only a handful of elite human operators” have ever been able to pull off stunts as you see in the demo videos.

    The technology behind the remarkable acrobatic skid-steer is mostly Reinforcement Learning (RL), with physics modeling and neural network models. As machinery like this is so significant, powerful, and bulky, undertaking RL directly on the hardware wasn’t deemed practical. Instead, the research team decided to use a simulation programmed with the John Deere 332G’s complex array of controls for training. This data was subsequently applied to the actual skid-steer via a sim-to-real transfer. The simulations must be extremely accurate.

    It has been revealed that this acrobatic goliath is impressive, but of course there’s an underlying goal driving Heavy Metal Acrobatics’ research. The scientists are laying the foundations for the enabling of “dynamic autonomous control of heavy machinery.” It is hoped this will help promote greater automation in heavy equipment sectors of industry. Eventually, autonomous control should be safer, faster, and more efficient than any human.

    With these video demonstrations of nimble and highly maneuverable heavy machinery, it is clear that there’s more scope for AI-driven automation than one may have previously expected. Furthermore, it looks like being a skilled heavy machinery operator is definitely not an AI-proof occupation.

    📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2360 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sitepoint

    💡 Key Takeaways

    • Setting up WireGuard on a small virtual server is a satisfying infrastructure task.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

    Setting up WireGuard on a small virtual server is a satisfying infrastructure task. Install the package, generate a key pair, open a UDP port, configure a peer, and connect a laptop. Within an afternoon, your staging environment can sit behind a private tunnel, and your internal dashboard can be restricted to traffic from a known address.

    The initial setup is rarely the difficult part.

    The real engineering work starts when the team changes. A developer joins, another leaves, someone replaces a laptop, a server needs patching, or a connection suddenly stops working. Each event creates a small maintenance task. Over time, those tasks become an operational responsibility that somebody must own.

    This article examines what it takes to operate a self-hosted WireGuard VPN for a development team. We'll look at peer configuration, access management, troubleshooting, monitoring tools, and the engineering time involved. We'll also compare self-hosting with managed business VPN services so teams can make a decision based on their infrastructure needs.

    WireGuard is a modern VPN protocol designed to establish encrypted connections between network peers. Its relatively small codebase, modern cryptography, and straightforward configuration make it attractive for developers who want control over their network infrastructure.

    A basic WireGuard deployment typically involves:.

    A server with a reachable public IP address.

    A private and public key pair for the server.

    A key pair for every client device.

    A UDP port through which peers communicate.

    Peer configuration that defines which addresses are allowed through the tunnel.

    A simplified server configuration might look like this:.

    The corresponding client configuration contains the client's private key and the server's public key:.

    These examples illustrate the basic relationship between a server and a client. A production configuration will also need appropriate firewall rules, routing, DNS settings, and a plan for distributing configuration securely.

    It has been revealed that the important distinction is that WireGuard establishes encrypted peer connections. It does not automatically provide a complete employee identity system, onboarding workflow, approval process, or audit dashboard.

    Those responsibilities belong to the team operating the infrastructure.

    Developers interested in using WireGuard on personal development devices can also explore SitePoint's guide to building a hardened mobile development environment with Termux, Docker, and WireGuard.

    A peer is not just an entry in a configuration file. It represents a device that has permission to communicate through your network.

    That makes peer management an access-control responsibility.

    In a recent development, for a small development team, it is tempting to keep a single configuration file and enhancement it manually whenever someone joins or leaves. This can work initially, but it becomes harder to manage as the number of devices increases.

    A useful first step is to maintain a peer inventory:.

    In a recent development, the inventory should not contain private keys. Private keys must remain on their respective devices and should never be placed in a shared spreadsheet or source repository.

    The inventory instead helps administrators answer practical questions:.

    Which person owns this public key?

    Which device is associated with this tunnel address?

    Is the device still authorized?

    When was its access last reviewed?

    Has the peer been removed after the device was lost or replaced?

    This information becomes especially crucial when a team uses the VPN to reach staging servers, internal dashboards, databases, or other development resources.

    Manual onboarding is manageable when a team has only two or three developers. It becomes unreliable when several people join, leave, or change devices over the year.

    A repeatable onboarding process should cover more than generating a key pair.

    A practical workflow looks like this:.

    Confirm that the team member is authorized to access the environment.

    Generate a key pair on the user's device.

    Assign a unique tunnel address.

    Add the public key to the server's peer configuration.

    Apply the appropriate routing and firewall permissions.

    Deliver the client configuration through a secure channel.

    Test access to the specific development resources the person needs.

    Record the peer owner, device, and approval details.

    Offboarding needs an equally clear process:.

    Identify every peer associated with the departing team member.

    Remove the relevant public keys from the server.

    Confirm that the configuration change has been applied.

    Review any other credentials or allowlists that granted access.

    Record when access was revoked.

    An administrator can inspect the currently configured peers with:.

    According to recent reports, the output helps identify peer public keys, transfer counters, and latest handshake information. It is useful for troubleshooting, but it should not be treated as a complete access audit or proof that a particular person is still authorized.

    The broader lesson is to make access changes part of a documented workflow. A peer should not remain active simply because nobody remembers who created it.

    One common network-design mistake is assuming that connecting to a VPN should give a developer access to every internal service.

    That is not necessarily the right model.

    A developer working on a frontend application may need access to a staging web server but not to the production database. A contractor may need access to one test environment without being able to reach internal administration tools.

    WireGuard's peer configuration and the surrounding network controls should be designed around those requirements.

    For example, teams can combine:.

    Separate tunnel address ranges for different groups.

    Firewall rules that restrict traffic to approved services.

    Cloud security groups that limit access to specific ports.

    Application-level authentication for internal dashboards.

    Separate production and staging network boundaries.

    In a recent development, the exact implementation depends on the infrastructure. The key point is that VPN membership and application authorization are different controls.

    A successful VPN handshake should not be treated as permission to access every resource behind the tunnel.

    Recent findings suggest that A VPN can appear simple when it works. Diagnosing it becomes more complicated when a developer is connecting from a home router, a hotel network, or a mobile hotspot.

    DNS resolving to an unexpected address.

    Incorrect routing or AllowedIPs settings.

    Firewall rules blocking UDP traffic.

    MTU problems that affect larger packets.

    A peer using an outdated configuration.

    A server process or host becoming unavailable.

    WireGuard provides useful inspection commands:.

    These commands help inspect peer information, check the service state, and review recent service logs. The exact systemd service name can differ depending on how the interface was configured.

    Recent findings suggest that administrators should also monitor the underlying server. At minimum, that means checking:.

    Whether the WireGuard interface is active.

    Whether the UDP port is reachable.

    Whether disk or memory usage is approaching a limit.

    Whether operating-system and package updates are pending.

    A small virtual server may be inexpensive, but it is still infrastructure that needs an owner.

    Industry observers note that teams working with alternative tunnel-based development workflows may find SitePoint's tutorial on setting up Cloudflare Tunnels with Docker Compose for persistent webhook debugging useful. It covers a different tunneling use case, but the operational questions around connectivity, service health, and troubleshooting are closely related.

    According to recent reports, A self-hosted VPN does not need to become a collection of manual tasks. A few established tools can make configuration, monitoring, and debugging more repeatable.

    The core tool is, of course, WireGuard. Its command-line utilities allow administrators to inspect peers, manage interfaces, and review connection information. The official documentation is the best starting point for understanding configuration options and platform support.

    Industry observers note that ansible can automate repeatable server administration tasks. A team could use playbooks to deploy configuration files, apply system updates, or standardize firewall settings across several VPN hosts.

    According to recent reports, sensitive values should be handled with an appropriate secrets-management approach. Private keys should not be committed to a Git repository or stored in plaintext playbooks.

    Prometheus is useful for collecting and querying metrics, while Node Exporter exposes Linux host metrics such as CPU, memory, disk, and network statistics.

    According to recent reports, these tools do not automatically provide a complete WireGuard security audit. They can, however, help identify resource problems and server-health problems before those problems become user-reported outages.

    Industry observers note that uptime Kuma provides a self-hosted monitoring dashboard with notifications. It can help teams monitor the availability of a VPN host or related services.

    A basic availability check does not prove that every VPN peer can connect successfully. For more meaningful monitoring, combine host checks with an end-to-end test from a separate network.

    Wireshark and tcpdump help developers inspect network traffic when diagnosing connectivity problems.

    For example, tcpdump can capture UDP traffic on the WireGuard port:.

    Recent findings suggest that this can help determine whether packets are reaching the server. It does not decrypt WireGuard traffic or replace checks of routing, firewall rules, and peer configuration.

    The right toolset depends on the size of the deployment. A team with one VPN server may only need WireGuard's own commands and basic host monitoring. A larger environment may benefit from automation, centralized metrics, and a documented incident process.

    In a recent development, A self-hosted VPN can cost very little in direct infrastructure charges. However, the server invoice does not include the engineering time required to operate it.

    Consider a hypothetical team with these assumptions:.

    Two people join and two leave during the year.

    The team reviews or rotates device keys quarterly.

    Patching and monitoring require about two hours per month.

    Six troubleshooting incidents occur annually.

    The estimated loaded engineering cost is $60 per hour.

    The virtual server costs approximately $6 per month.

    The following estimate illustrates how quickly maintenance time can exceed the infrastructure bill.

    At $60 per hour, 46 hours represent approximately $2,760 in engineering time. The server adds around $72 per year, bringing the estimated total to $2,832.

    These figures are illustrative, not a universal cost benchmark. A team with infrastructure automation and established monitoring may spend considerably less time. A team with frequent staff changes or strict audit requirements may spend more.

    Recent findings suggest that the useful exercise is to measure the work your own team performs. Track onboarding, access reviews, patching, incidents, and recovery time for a few months. That gives you a more realistic comparison than looking at hosting prices alone.

    Self-hosting is not automatically the best option just because a team has developers who can configure servers.

    A managed business VPN may be worth considering when the team needs centralized member management, simpler device administration, or a stable network exit address without maintaining the underlying VPN infrastructure.

    Depending on the provider and proposal, managed services may offer:.

    A central dashboard for adding and removing users.

    Dedicated or shared IP options.

    Client applications for common operating systems.

    Multi-factor authentication or identity integrations.

    Centralized administration and support.

    For example, PureVPN for Teams is one service in this category. Teams evaluating it—or any other provider—should check the current feature set, pricing, logging practices, access controls, and service terms before making a decision.

    Sources indicate that A managed service does not remove every security responsibility. The team still needs to decide who receives access, review permissions, protect user accounts, and understand how traffic and metadata are handled.

    It also introduces vendor dependency and a recurring subscription cost. Those trade-offs should be considered alongside the engineering time saved.

    There are situations where running WireGuard yourself is the more practical option.

    You already operate infrastructure. If your team routinely patches servers, manages secrets, monitors services, and responds to incidents, maintaining a VPN may add relatively little work.

    It has been revealed that you need custom routing. A deployment that connects several private cloud networks, on-premises environments, or specialized subnets may require network controls that are easier to implement directly.

    You have strict data-control requirements. Some organizations have policies that limit which third parties can handle network traffic or related metadata. Those requirements may favor infrastructure under the organization's own control.

    Industry observers note that you have a dedicated platform or security team. If someone is explicitly responsible for access management, monitoring, and incident response, self-hosting can fit naturally into existing operations.

    You can automate the lifecycle. Infrastructure-as-code, configuration management, documented peer inventories, and tested recovery procedures can reduce repetitive work and make a self-hosted deployment easier to maintain.

    The crucial distinction is between a deliberately operated service and a one-off server that nobody owns.

    Before choosing an approach, ask the following questions:.

    Who is responsible for the VPN six or twelve months after deployment?

    How many people and devices are likely to join or leave?

    How are public keys and peer configurations tracked?

    How quickly can access be revoked when a device is lost?

    Which internal services should each developer be able to reach?

    Do you need a fixed egress IP for external allowlists?

    What monitoring and recovery process exists if the server fails?

    Do your customers or internal policies require access logs or formal reviews?

    Does your team have the time and expertise to maintain the infrastructure?

    Would a managed service cost less than the engineering time and operational risk it replaces?

    If your team already has mature infrastructure practices and needs custom network control, self-hosting may be a sensible choice.

    If the team is small, access changes frequently, and nobody has time to own another server, a managed service may be more practical.

    Sources indicate that wireGuard is an excellent protocol, and deploying it can be a straightforward engineering task. But operating a VPN for a development team involves more than establishing an encrypted connection.

    Peer management, onboarding, offboarding, network permissions, monitoring, patching, and troubleshooting all require ongoing attention.

    The right choice depends on the team's infrastructure experience, security requirements, size, and available engineering time. Self-hosting offers control and flexibility; a managed service can reduce operational work. Neither option removes the need for sound access-control practices.

    Before deciding, calculate the maintenance effort, identify who will own the service, and make sure the design can be maintained as the team changes.

    The cost example uses illustrative assumptions rather than current vendor pricing. Managed VPN features and prices can change, so verify provider details before purchasing.

    Rockstar released GTA 6 on November 19 for PS5 and Xbox Series X|S, ending a 13-year wait for a latest numbered Grand Theft Auto.

    But while players are only just getting their first look at Vice City and the rest of Leonida, some are already looking ahead to the next entry in the series.

    On launch day, Zelnick joined the TBPN podcast to talk about the release, and was asked early on about when GTA 7 could drop, to which he answered: “Once you get through several hundred hours of the most incredible fun you’ve ever heard, ask the question again.”.

    Later in the interview, he was asked about the sequel again and how major the map could be, given that GTA 6 covers a huge city and a surrounding state.

    “Theoretically, GTA 7 could just be a live version of the entire world, right?” one of the hosts asked, with Zelnick clearly amused by the question.

    Industry observers note that “We at Take-Two just went live with GTA 6 on November 19,” he jokingly replied. “Let me check my watch. Oh, it’s still November 19. And you’re asking a question about GTA 7. I mean guys, really?”.

    Recent findings suggest that jordi: "Theoretically, GTA 7 could just be a live version of the entire world, right?"@StraussZelnick, the CEO behind GTA 6: "We went live with GTA 6 on November 19. Let me check my watch. Oh, it's still November 19. And you're asking a question about GTA 7." pic.twitter.com/sHdVawdln2.

    He then mentioned a quote his father used to say about past achievements being “yesterday’s headlines,” but then quipped: “It’s not even yesterday.”.

    According to recent reports, with GTA 6 only just arriving, it will likely be years before we get any concrete information about its potential follow-up. However, Zelnick has hinted that Rockstar’s future games won’t take as long to make.

    Plus, we still have GTA 6 Online to look forward to, which should tide players over until GTA 7.

    A brand-new phone that doesn’t connect to the internet has been debuted in Japan, and it looks like the classic Nokia phones that you might remember.

    For years, smartphone consumers have been trying to find creative solutions to cut down their screen time, especially as phones have started doing weekly reviews of app usage and screen time.

    Some have opted to set time limits on the apps they can use, while others have created heavyweight cases that will quite literally force you to work out in order to use your smartphone.

    In other cases, some people have taken a step back in time, ditching their smartphones for flip phones and devices that don’t actually connect to the internet. These throwback phones have popped up across Europe and the United States, and now Japan is getting in on the act with a upcoming device.

    As per The Japan Times, Japan’s KDDI Corporation has introduced a mobile phone with “minimal functions.”.

    It has been revealed that named the Infobar Zero, it will be available to pick up on Christmas Day, and is limited to calls, text messages, and other basic features. Owners won’t have the ability to connect to the internet, but it will have a camera and a music player.

    While it isn’t a complete recreation of Nokia’s iconic 3310 phone, the Infobar Zero does strike up plenty of comparisons to that classic device.

    Additionally, the ‘dumbphone’ isn’t aimed at replacing your smartphone, but rather providing a break from the smartphone life.

    It has been planned by KDDI for quite some time, just as a way of relieving the reliance to live life on apps.

    Owners will be able to register their phone numbers on the Zero and a smartphone as part of KDDI’s “two numbers” system – sort of like using an eSIM in some parts of the world.

    Microsoft outage brings fax machines back into action across Japanese offices.

    $499 flip phone that blocks all social media revealed by console maker Commodore.

    This new phone is built to break your social media addiction.

    You will be able to keep your smartphone at home when you go to school or work, and then return to using it later in the day, if that’s how you choose to live.

    Elsewhere, a new app called Island has been introduced, and the farming simulator-like game will actually punish you for spending too much time on it.

    OpenAI's AI models boost AMD's upcoming flagship GPU design by up to 14% in PPA

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (572 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that openAI just revealed latest details about its ongoing partnership with AMD, in which engineers used undisclosed AI models to help optimize the hardware maker's upcoming flagship GPU and CPU designs.
    • OpenAI says that its model spotted "further improvements by rewriting the code that describes the chip’s circuits." This work was done in SystemVerilog RTL, the language commonly used for high-end chip design.
    • Furthermore, OpenAI claims its model was reasoning on RTL "at the level of an expert microarchitect," and that it expects to squeeze further PPA improvements in both GPU and CPU designs, up from the now-improved baseline.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that openAI just revealed latest details about its ongoing partnership with AMD, in which engineers used undisclosed AI models to help optimize the hardware maker's upcoming flagship GPU and CPU designs. The leading figures are up to 14% PPA (power, performance, and area) improvement for the GPU circuitry, and unspecified single-digit PPA gains on the processor.

    OpenAI says that its model spotted "further improvements by rewriting the code that describes the chip’s circuits." This work was done in SystemVerilog RTL, the language commonly used for high-end chip design. The firm claims that its model's optimization efforts are equivalent to condensing a year's worth of conventional chip design work into "under 5 months" — a time crunch it says is unprecedented in this arena.

    Furthermore, OpenAI claims its model was reasoning on RTL "at the level of an expert microarchitect," and that it expects to squeeze further PPA improvements in both GPU and CPU designs, up from the now-improved baseline.

    It has been revealed that this isn't AI's first time working on chips. It worked with Broadcom on designing OpenAI Jalapeño, an inference-targeted chip that was already running actual workloads with engineering samples as far back as June 2026.

    Industry observers note that the company expected to have small initial Jalapeño deployments around late 2026, and pinned a broader rollout to 2027. Test benchmarks have been out for a while, displaying purported excellent savings on power draw and overall latency versus the market-leading Nvidia Blackwell GPUs in single-token prediction workloads.

    According to recent reports, the blog post also explains how GPT's chip-design acumen evolved. The researchers tested its high-end LLMs by asking them to improve PicoRV32 and Ibex chip cores. The models were given 112,000 tokens per run, told to optimize for throughput (a combination of Instructions-per-Clock and clock-cycle duration), and scored the results.

    It has been revealed that A fat zero was given if the chips didn't work or used more than 16x the previous area, and 1.0 was given for the best designs under the test constraints. The test also didn't tell the models which workloads the chips were going to be used for. As expected, GPT-6.2 Astra had by far the best showing, on both axes: both the lowest overall cost and the highest optimization score.

    Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

    A second test also revealed an interesting but unsurprising fact: the models provided better results when essentially redesigning the chips according to their initial specifications, rather than optimizing existing code.

    In a recent development, there's no word on whether the scientists used unmodified versions of GPT to perform this work. Task-specific high-end LLMs exist for those who can afford them, and OpenAI itself says it's working with Synopsys to train GPT-Synopsis, a model for using chip design tools.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    GTA 6 players are reporting crashes on PS5 and Xbox, with some even unable to get past the opening minutes of the game.

    While many GTA 6 fans across PlayStation and Xbox are enjoying their time in Leonida, it’s not all sunshine and rainbows for everyone trying to explore Rockstar’s latest installment.

    Since its November 19 release, players have reported game-breaking crashes that prevent them from progressing through the main story and even playing altogether.

    In a Reddit post, one PS5 player noted the game had worked flawlessly until they reached Pipework, one of the game’s early missions, where you are introduced to Mandy.

    Industry observers note that “It crashes every time I use the plunger or stand around the sink with it,” they wrote, adding that they can no longer progress through the story. “You would think the plane flying was intensive, but it crashes every time I use the plunger or stand around the sink with it. I just paid $125 for my PS5 to be repaired and $100 for the game, this is ridiculous.”.

    Others are running into problems much earlier, with a PS5 Pro owner revealing the game crashes as the opening prologue begins.

    In a recent development, “Game keeps crashing at the exact same point during the opening prologue. I’m using a PS5 Pro and have been unable to play since launch. The game crashes immediately as the startup prologue begins, either at the exact same point or a couple of seconds into it, displaying error code CE-108255-1.”.

    When checking the PlayStation Support page, error CE-108255-1 prompts players to simply “try updating your game”. However, GTA 6 fans who have encountered this issue on PS5 have reported that clearing the console’s cache, rebuilding its database, factory resetting the PS5, and downloading the game three times has done nothing to alleviate the problem.

    “Despite all this, the issue persists. It crashes at the same point every single time,” they wrote. “I’m honestly extremely disappointed and frustrated at this point. I’ve exhausted almost every troubleshooting step available online and still haven’t been able to play.”.

    Industry observers note that the reports are not limited to PlayStation, either, as some Xbox Series X players have also reported crashes within minutes of play. “The game sometimes even crashes after only 15 minutes. The first crash happened about 2 hours after I started playing, and ever since that it kept crashing,” added another player.

    Rockstar’s GTA 6 troubleshooting page currently directs players experiencing console errors to PlayStation or Xbox support, but hopefully a patch will fix this issue sooner rather than later.

    According to recent reports, animal control was forced to respond to a call about an alligator on the loose, but it turned out to be just a pool floatie. Seriously.

    Over the years, plenty of people have rushed to call emergency services to report something that, when investigated, turned out to be totally false.

    It has been revealed that this was the case over in Sugar Land, Texas, on November 12 when animal control received a call about an alligator being on the loose. As per Sugar Land Animal Services, they were told that the gator appeared to be feeling a bit sick and in need of some assistance.

    Yet, when they reached it, it wasn’t all it seemed. “When ASO Perez arrived on the scene to investigate, she was in for a big surprise. What looked very real from a distance turned out to be a runaway pool floatie!” they posted on Facebook.

    “While this call definitely gave our team a good laugh, we always take every report seriously,” Animal Services added.

    According to recent reports, in the photo, the inflatable gator had its mouth stuck open with teeth on show, so if you see it from a distance, you might be confused. However, up close, you can tell it’s meant to be lounged on, not hunted or scared of.

    “Remember: if you ever spot wildlife that looks sick or injured, please keep a safe distance and call the experts to handle it. You never know if it’s the real deal!”.

    Naturally, commenters saw the funny side of things too. “Well, that was a rather inflated story then,” one joked. “She is very brave! Thank you, Officer Perez, for all you do,” another added. “Wow. It looks so realistic! Crazy,” another replied.

    As noted, it isn’t the first instance of floaties being reported as real, nor is it the wildest.

    #93366. Latest Update: The Design Workflow Is Broken. Here Is How Vitalii Khomenko Thinks It Should Be Fixed

    📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1742 w)

    Latest Update: The Design Workflow Is Broken. Here Is How Vitalii Khomenko Thinks It Should Be Fixed

    📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1742 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sitepoint

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.
    • Industry observers note that 7 Day Free Trial.
    • It has been revealed that with 250+ client engagements across both agency and embedded in-house roles, Vitalii Khomenko has seen product teams from the inside in a way few designers have.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

    Weekly. Free. One click to leave.

    It has been revealed that with 250+ client engagements across both agency and embedded in-house roles, Vitalii Khomenko has seen product teams from the inside in a way few designers have. Here he makes the case for a new kind of design workflow built for the AI era, and explains why the window to adapt is narrower than most founders think.

    For the last decade, every startup conversation about speed eventually became a conversation about engineering. Hiring more developers, cutting scope, choosing a simpler stack, it was almost always a dev-side problem. Vitalii Khomenko, Principal Designer at Orizon Design and founder of Fluente LLC, argues that's no longer true. And he has a specific view on what teams should do instead.

    According to recent reports, what makes Khomenko's perspective worth taking seriously isn't just seniority. It's the specific shape of his experience. Over a career spanning 250+ client engagements, he has worked both as an external specialist brought in to deliver and as an embedded designer who became the single connective thread between product, brand, and execution. That dual vantage point is rare. Most designers live on one side of that line. Khomenko has operated extensively on both, which gives him an unusually clear read on where friction actually originates inside product teams, and where it doesn't.

    Sources indicate that his work spans early-stage startups finding their first visual language and established brands managing complex, multi-disciplinary design systems. Across that range, certain patterns repeat. And the pattern that started becoming impossible to ignore this year pointed him toward a conclusion that is reshaping how he thinks a modern design workflow should actually be structured.

    The bottleneck didn't disappear. It moved. And the workflow needs to move with it.

    In a recent development, when shipping code was slow, the existing design workflow made sense. Multiple rounds of revision, user testing, iteration, all of that fit naturally into the window while engineering caught up. That window is now gone, and most design workflows were never updated to reflect it.

    "Founders are asking design teams to move at the same speed as an AI-assisted dev pipeline, and design doesn't compress the same way code does," Khomenko says. The result is a workflow that was built around a constraint that no longer exists, applied to a pipeline that has fundamentally changed around it.

    The forced choice between polish and speed that product teams are now navigating isn't new as a concept. What's new is how stark it has become, and how directly it traces back to a workflow problem rather than a people problem. "Because development is cheap and fast now, there's constant pressure to ship the next thing immediately," he explains. "But the products that actually retain customers are still the ones where the details were considered carefully. Fewer revision rounds isn't a process improvement if it means shipping avoidable friction.".

    Khomenko has watched this play out across enough teams, at enough stages, to be specific about where the existing workflow breaks down. The issue isn't design judgment. It's where that judgment sits in the process, and what format it's expected to produce at the end.

    According to recent reports, to understand Khomenko's proposed fix, it helps to understand exactly where the current workflow stalls. For most product teams, the end of the design process looks like this: a designer produces polished, dev-ready screens inside Figma, and hands that file to engineering. Engineering then interprets those screens, translates the visual decisions into code, and builds from there.

    That translation step, Figma file to working code, is where the pipeline now breaks down. AI-assisted engineering has made the building part dramatically faster. But the translation step hasn't changed. An engineer still has to read a Figma file, interpret spacing, extract assets, make judgment calls about component structure, and write the implementation from scratch. That process takes the same amount of time it always did.

    "The manual workflow inside Figma simply isn't keeping up with AI-boosted engineering," Khomenko says. "The design handoff is quietly becoming the thing everyone is waiting on.".

    It has been revealed that the result is a pipeline where everything around the handoff has accelerated, and the handoff itself has become the single point of drag. Figma, in other words, was built for a world where engineering was the slow part. It wasn't designed to feed a pipeline where engineering moves at AI speed.

    This is the core of what Khomenko is proposing, and it's a more significant structural shift than it might first appear.

    In his workflow, Figma doesn't disappear. It moves. Rather than serving as both the exploration environment and the final delivery artifact, Figma becomes the visual exploration layer exclusively: the place where brand identity is established, layout logic is worked through, and design direction is validated. It remains the right tool for figuring out what something should look and feel like.

    Recent findings suggest that but the final delivery, the artifact that actually goes to engineering, is code. Specifically, components built into prepared libraries that engineering can work from and scale directly, without any translation step in between.

    The difference in implementation speed is the point. When a designer delivers a coded component library rather than a Figma file, engineering doesn't need to interpret anything. The decisions are already expressed in the language they're building in. What previously required an engineer to read, interpret, and re-create from a visual reference now arrives ready to use. In a pipeline running on AI-assisted development, that difference compounds fast.

    "Figma is still the right place to explore what something should look and feel like," Khomenko notes. "But handing over a Figma file and asking engineering to implement it is now the slow path. Delivering in code is the fast path. That's the shift.".

    Industry observers note that executing this workflow requires a different kind of designer, and Khomenko is direct about that. The UI/UX designer becoming a Design Engineer is, in his assessment, not a distant possibility. It is a matter of time, and the teams treating it as a future consideration rather than a present reality are the ones most likely to find themselves stuck at the handoff.

    In a recent development, but Khomenko is equally clear about what this shift doesn't mean. Delivering in code is one part of the role, not the whole of it. The full design cycle isn't going anywhere. Applying branding to imagery, producing animations, building marketing materials, these remain essential creative tasks that require a broad and varied toolkit well beyond code. "The designer of the near future isn't just generating code," he claims. "They're moving across the full cycle, brand, motion, marketing, product, with design engineering as an important and growing part of that stack, not a replacement for it.".

    What changes is that code-ready delivery becomes a core expectation within that stack. The designer who can move fluidly from visual exploration in Figma to component delivery in code, while also carrying the brand thinking, motion, and marketing creativity that differentiates products at the surface level consumers actually experience, is the profile that the new workflow demands.

    Recent findings suggest that khomenko is candid that no single version of this workflow has fully standardized yet. Every team is figuring it out differently. The tools are evolving, the handoff expectations are shifting, and the processes teams are building around all of it vary considerably. There is no off-the-shelf playbook.

    But this is precisely where his 250+ engagements become more than a credential. They're a dataset. Having watched enough teams, at enough stages, through enough cycles of tooling change, Khomenko can see through the noise of individual variation and identify what's directionally true even when the specifics are still in flux. "Each team's workflow is really custom at this stage," he says. "But some general patterns of how this is going to look in the near future are already visible.".

    Those patterns consistently point in the same direction: design judgment moving earlier, final delivery moving into code, and the designer's role expanding in technical range while staying broad in creative scope. The exact tools and sequences will keep shifting. The underlying logic of the workflow Khomenko is describing is already taking shape in the teams paying closest attention.

    For founders and product leads, the workflow Khomenko is describing has direct implications for how teams are staffed, budgeted, and structured.

    Industry observers note that front-load design judgment. The biggest leverage in the upcoming workflow isn't faster execution, it's better problem definition before generation starts. Bring senior design thinking in earlier, when it can shape what gets built rather than polish what's already done.

    Separate exploration from delivery. Figma and the visual exploration phase serve a distinct purpose from the final delivery layer. Treat them as separate stages with separate expectations, rather than collapsing them into a single step expected to produce everything.

    Shift the delivery expectation to code. Whether that means hiring for Design Engineer range, developing it internally, or restructuring handoffs, the end of the design pipeline needs to arrive in a form engineering can work from directly. The translation step is where time goes to die, and it's now the most avoidable part of the process.

    According to recent reports, protect the full creative stack. Design engineering matters more than it ever has. It is not, however, the whole job. Teams that reduce design to code generation will lose the brand thinking, motion, and marketing creativity that differentiates products at the surface level users actually experience.

    Stay flexible. The workflow is still forming. Teams that build rigidity into their process now will find themselves redoing that work within a year. The teams getting this right are the ones building enough adaptability into their structures to absorb what's still coming.

    "The Figma handoff made sense when engineering was the slow part," Khomenko notes. "Engineering isn't the slow part anymore. Delivering in code isn't the future of design workflow. For the teams paying attention, it's already the present.".

    • Sources indicate that A Redditor from the UK was flying from the United States with their desktop PC in a carry-on but was forced to check it.

    • It has been revealed that the desktop PC only had a bag and several layers of protective wrapping for protection.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that A Redditor from the UK was flying from the United States with their desktop PC in a carry-on but was forced to check it. According to u/FattyLeopold, they’ve carried their PC as a carry-on on different flights, and they brought it with them in the cabin all the way across the Atlantic. The trip even included a layover.

    Industry observers note that “It was 4am, and I was pissed off,” the Redditor replied to one comment. “Just said fu-- it, let’s see what happens. Probably confused the universe a bit, ‘Dude… what are you doing… Aight, have it your way.’” They then taped the PC, monitor, and keyboard together in the package.

    It has been revealed that the desktop PC only had a bag and several layers of protective wrapping for protection. What’s more surprising is that the owner didn’t even take the GPU off its bracket and put it in their carry-on. When they arrived at their destination, they recorded the “unboxing” of their PC. Against all odds, their computer arrived without a single dent or scratch — the tempered glass on the side of the PC didn’t even shatter after the possible trauma it went through in baggage handling.

    Most of us have seen videos of airport baggage handlers throwing bags and packages around while they’re loading them onto the plane, not to mention the bumps and tumbles that luggage takes when going through an airport’s baggage conveyor system. The PC also has to deal with the vibration and turbulence of flight. The shortest direct flight across the pond is about 6 hours and 30 minutes — since the Redditor said that they had a layover, that meant that the desktop PC had been in transit for a bit longer than that.

    It’s a miracle that the computer was able to make it through the journey without a scratch, but the Redditor is not out of the woods yet. They noted that even though the computer looked undamaged on the surface, they haven’t been able to boot it yet because they do not have a proper adapter for outlets in the UK. Hopefully, they could get it working after finding the right plug or adapter for their computer, or with some basic troubleshooting (like re-plugging the components) if it won’t turn on after the first try. GPUs and memory sticks are quite expensive these days, after all, and it’s unlikely that AMD would replace their graphics card because of this misadventure, unlike this $10,000 RTX Pro 6000 that Nvidia replaced after a customer who bought it upcoming broke the GPU in transit.

    Chipotle is bringing back its Thanksgiving BOGO promotion, giving customers a chance to score a free meal ahead of the holiday.

    The fast food chain announced on November 20 that its Back Home BOGO deal will return for one night only, allowing Rewards members to get two meals for the price of one at participating US restaurants.

    Industry observers note that the promotion first introduced in 2025 and became Chipotle’s largest sales-driving campaign of the year. Its return comes as millions of Americans prepare to travel home and reconnect with friends and family over Thanksgiving weekend.

    According to recent reports, on Wednesday, November 25, Chipotle Rewards members can receive a free meal when purchasing another one of equal or greater value between 5 p.m. and 9 p.m. local time.

    To redeem the offer, customers must visit a participating US Chipotle restaurant and scan their Rewards membership card at checkout.

    The promotion is available exclusively in restaurants, meaning orders placed through the Chipotle app, website, delivery services, or third-party platforms will not qualify.

    Industry observers note that customers can receive up to five free meals per check, provided they purchase an meal of equal or greater value for each free item. Kids’ meals do not count toward the promotion.

    “Thanksgiving Eve is when the hometown group chat comes to life,” noted Stephanie Perdue, Chipotle’s Senior Vice President of Brand Marketing.

    Recent findings suggest that “Whether Chipotle is the first stop of the night or where the crew ends up later, we’re giving friends a place to get together over real food. The response last year revealed us how much our guests embraced the occasion, and we’re excited to bring it back as another reason for hometown crews to reconnect before Thanksgiving.”.

    Chipotle is giving away free food to anyone with a tattoo for one hour only.

    Chipotle is offering $6 entrees on Halloween to customers who wear costumes.

    Chipotle launches School Spirit BOGO with free entrees for back-to-school season.

    The company cited Morning Consult research showing that 76% of Gen Z consumers visit restaurants to socialize with friends and family, highlighting the role dining out plays in holiday gatherings.

    Chipotle is also offering a separate promotion following Thanksgiving, giving customers a $0 delivery fee on qualifying orders from November 27 through November 30.

    According to recent reports, to claim the delivery offer, customers must enter the code CYBER26 when ordering through Chipotle’s app or website. The deal requires a minimum purchase of $10 in the US or $12 in Canada, excluding taxes and fees.

    Although the delivery fee will be waived, customers may still face higher menu prices and additional service fees.

    Both promotions are available for a limited time at participating locations, with the Thanksgiving BOGO ending at 9 p.m. local time on November 25.

    The cards were from Pokemon’s 30th Celebration expansion, which launched on September 16 with 30 different foil Pikachu cards, one in each booster pack. The set arrived weeks after Walmart began holding online drawings for some Pokemon card releases.

    Recent findings suggest that officers responded to a report of a theft in progress at the Dodgeville Walmart Supercenter shortly after 11:15 a.m. local time on November 19. They pulled over a black Tesla with Florida plates and said a search turned up 125 packages of 30th Celebration boosters.

    Police also recovered 112 packages of One Piece trading cards, 26 Pokemon anniversary tin sets, and a Rayquaza Lego set, along with other merchandise still in its packaging.

    In a recent development, police mentioned the Tesla had traveled to several locations in Wisconsin and Minnesota, as well as Missouri. The department is asking other agencies to come forward if they can link any of the additional merchandise to thefts in their area.

    In a separate case in September, an Ohio collector was sentenced to 90 days of GPS monitoring after putting a tracker on a van used to deliver Pokemon cards to Walmart.

    When Should You Remove NAT from an On-Prem Kubernetes Network?

    📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1144 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sitepoint

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.
    • Industry observers note that weekly.
    • In a recent development, in an on-premises Kubernetes environment, removing NAT can make the network simpler to inspect, reduce translation overhead, and let the data center route directly to workloads.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

    Industry observers note that weekly. Free. One click to leave.

    7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

    In a recent development, in an on-premises Kubernetes environment, removing NAT can make the network simpler to inspect, reduce translation overhead, and let the data center route directly to workloads. But direct routing is not automatically the right choice.

    Sources indicate that the decision depends on what the organization controls and what it needs from the network. A team that owns the physical fabric, has enough address space, and is comfortable operating BGP may benefit from making pod networks directly routable. A smaller environment, a team without control of the underlay, or a cluster that benefits from network abstraction may be better served by NAT or an overlay.

    Kubernetes is also changing the ground under these decisions: kube-proxy is set to drop IPVS support starting with version 1.43, with nftables as the replacement. For on-prem teams already reviewing their service data path, it is a good moment to ask whether NAT still belongs in it.

    So the useful question is not how to eliminate NAT, but when the operational benefits of doing so justify the additional routing responsibility.

    NAT solves a real problem. It allows an internal network to use its own address space without requiring the surrounding infrastructure to know how to reach every endpoint inside it. This is especially useful when you don’t control the underlying network.

    However, an on-premises data center is different. When you control both the Kubernetes cluster and the surrounding physical network, you can make Kubernetes networks directly routable.

    According to recent reports, in our case, removing NAT had practical and architectural benefits. It improved network performance, reduced CPU load on the nodes, and removed the risk of conntrack tables filling up on Kubernetes hosts. A directly routed L3 model also works well for traffic balancing when a node has two uplinks.

    Recent findings suggest that this does not mean eliminating NAT from the data center entirely. NAT can remain at the boundary of the on-premises network, for example on hardware firewalls. Inside the data center, however, Kubernetes networks can be directly routable, allowing the physical network to reach workloads using the same routing mechanisms it already uses elsewhere.

    In our implementation, BGP connects the Kubernetes network to the data center fabric: BIRD runs on the nodes and advertises pod CIDRs and selected service addresses, while kube-router manages Kubernetes networking. We described this implementation in more detail in our earlier article on building a routable on-prem.

    In a recent development, kubernetes cluster with BGP and ECMP. The important point for this decision is not the particular stack, but the requirement it creates: the surrounding network must be able to accept and route Kubernetes prefixes safely. If the organization cannot or does not want to make the cluster part of its routing domain, keeping NAT or an overlay is usually the simpler choice.

    Recent findings suggest that removing NAT alone does not make a network resilient. If every node still depends on one switch, one NIC, or one uplink, direct routing simply exposes the same physical single point of failure more clearly.

    The resilience benefit appears when the physical topology supports multiple independent paths. In our setup, nodes connect to independent data center switches and ECMP can use equivalent routes across those paths. If one path disappears, traffic can continue over the other.

    In a recent development, that distinction matters when deciding whether direct routing is worth the effort. Organizations with redundant uplinks and switches can integrate Kubernetes into an already resilient routed fabric. If the underlay itself has no path redundancy, removing NAT should not be presented as a high-availability improvement: the physical failure domain still dominates the design.

    Our stack is one example of how direct routing can be implemented, not a default recommendation for clusters that remove NAT. We chose kube-router because it supports a minimal installation as a binary and systemd service and covers the networking functions we need for this L3 design. BIRD handles route advertisements to the surrounding network.

    Other environments may reasonably choose Calico for conventional L3 routing or Cilium when an eBPF-based dataplane and its additional capabilities are useful. The choice of CNI and routing daemon is secondary to the architectural decision: first decide whether exposing Kubernetes prefixes to the physical network makes operational sense, then choose the implementation that fits the team’s requirements.

    A directly routed Kubernetes network is not automatically better than an overlay or NAT-based architecture. Each model solves a different operational problem.

    Sources indicate that NAT is a reasonable choice when the cluster needs to remain isolated from the surrounding address blueprint, when pod addresses cannot be routed through the data center, or when the infrastructure team does not control the upstream network. It also keeps Kubernetes-specific prefixes out of the physical routing domain, which can be valuable for smaller environments where direct visibility into every pod is not important.

    An overlay is useful when portability and abstraction matter more than exposing the physical packet path. It lets Kubernetes networking remain largely independent of the underlay and can simplify deployment across heterogeneous infrastructure. The tradeoff is another layer to inspect during troubleshooting and, depending on the implementation, encapsulation overhead.

    It has been revealed that direct routing makes the most sense when the organization owns the physical network, has address space available for pod CIDRs, and has operators comfortable with BGP and route filtering. It becomes more attractive when preserving source addresses, using standard network troubleshooting tools, predictable performance, or integrating the cluster with redundant data center paths are vital. At a larger scale, those operational benefits can justify the extra coordination between Kubernetes and network teams.

    The broader lesson is not that every Kubernetes cluster needs BGP or that NAT should disappear everywhere. It is that Kubernetes has matured enough that we should stop automatically treating its network as a black box.

    As more production and AI workloads move onto Kubernetes, network architecture becomes part of application reliability. In an on-premises data center, BGP and ECMP give us the option to use the resilience already available in the physical network rather than building another isolated networking layer on top of it.

    Sometimes the best way to make Kubernetes networking more robust is not to add another abstraction, but to remove one. But only when the surrounding infrastructure and the team operating it are ready to take responsibility for the routing that abstraction previously hid.

    If most of those answers are yes, direct routing is worth serious consideration. If not, NAT or an overlay may be the more resilient operational choice—not because it is technically more advanced, but because it better matches the environment.

    The developers of One-armed Robber are asking players to spend their surprise refunds in the free Steam heist game after a hacker sent the money back without the studio’s permission.

    Duhndal released One-armed Robber in December 2023. The first-person game lets players rob banks and stores solo or with friends, with each robber limited to one arm. Crews can sneak into a vault or fight their way through, then haul out as much loot as they can carry. The game has roughly 54,000 Steam reviews, according to SteamDB.

    Industry observers note that on November 20, Duhndal noted someone gained access to one of its Steamworks API keys and used it to ban players and issue refunds for in-game purchases. The studio said the incident affected a small share of its player base.

    The refunds went to players who had never asked for their money back. Duhndal said the transactions caused “significant financial losses” for its small team. The studio gave no figure for the losses or how many refunds were issued.

    Duhndal asked players who want to help it recover to put some of their refund toward another purchase in One-armed Robber or one of the studio’s other games. It also confirmed a sale on heist maps for players looking to pick up missions they don’t already own.

    It has been revealed that “This is completely optional! You haven’t done anything wrong, and you don’t owe us anything,” the developer said.

    Duhndal stated it revoked the compromised key and lifted all unauthorized bans. Players who were unfairly banned should now be able to get back into the game.

    This Steam game wants you to beat it within two hours so you get a refund.

    Publisher blames “AI-slop” on Steam as their game only gets 15 players at launch.

    Developer claims 55,000 Steam players refunded game after beating it too fast.

    #93350. Breaking: XREAL Aura Initial Review: Taking Android XR out of the headset, but who is it for?

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2343 w)
    📖 Baca
    Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 9to5google ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: XREAL Aura Initial Review: Taking Android XR out of the headset, but who is it for?

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2343 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5google

    ⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • We all kind of want to be Tony Stark, don’t we?
    • XREAL isn’t new to the mixed reality space.
    • There are the glasses themselves which include two displays, one for each eye, and electrochromic dimming on the lenses to control just how much of the outer world you’re seeing.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    We all kind of want to be Tony Stark, don’t we? Almost everyone can relate to that futuristic sense of wonder that comes from the movies where we see digital elements being interacted with through a simple wave of the hand. To date, that’s only really been replicable through big ol’ headsets like Apple’s Vision Pro or the various Meta Quest sets. But with XREAL Aura, Android XR brings that feeling to something far easier to actually use, but my one remaining question is who this product is for.

    XREAL isn’t new to the mixed reality space. The firm has been building some of the best example of optical see-through XR glasses. These aren’t quite like a VR headset because they actually let you see the world around you, not through a camera, but by simply making the lenses themselves see-through. I’ve tried these in the past and, while they’re great for mirroring a tablet or laptop for bigger screen (especially on airplanes), I did feel they were missing something.

    But first, let’s talk hardware.

    XREAL Aura is a two-part device. There are the glasses themselves which include two displays, one for each eye, and electrochromic dimming on the lenses to control just how much of the outer world you’re seeing. It’s wildly different from a typical VR headset, while also having most of the same benefits. Unlike most other XREAL glasses, Aura has built-in world-facing cameras used for hand and spatial tracking, as well as being able to be used as a camera for things like scanning QR codes, Gemini Live, or simply taking a quick picture (there’s no privacy light here, but the bulkier-than-normal design compared to standard glasses is more than enough a dead giveaway that the “perv glasses” dilemma doesn’t really apply in my opinion).

    Sources indicate that the other half of the formula is a wired puck that provides battery power and the brains of Android XR. There’s no screen on the puck, just a status light, and it has USB-C out for the glasses as well as USB-C in for power and/or external devices. It also has a fingerprint sensor (are you hearing this Android tablet makers??) and a touchpad, the latter used as a secondary, far subtler input method within Android XR to supplement hand tracking.

    Together, these two make a wonderful package for building a true mixed reality experience. The displays are plenty bright for even the brightest indoor conditions (frankly, it’d be insane to use these outside in my opinion, though a wide-open plane window may present a challenge), and the electrochromic dimming does a great job of blocking out most, but not quite all of the world around you. If you’re looking to be fully cut off from reality as you would with a VR headset, these aren’t for you. I did find some display elements, like smaller text, a little tough to focus my eyes on at times, but I have a feeling that’s more so me being overdue for an eye exam than it is the glasses themselves. There’s virtually no flicker in my usage, with only bright white backgrounds occasionally being a little overbearing, and everything is smooth with the 120Hz refresh rate.

    Where this hardware really shines compared to a typical VR headset is in its design, and it’s what makes XREAL a perfect partner for Android XR. The glasses themselves weigh in at 95 grams, a mere fifth of the Meta Quest 3 and Samsung’s Galaxy XR, and up to 700 grams less than Apple’s Vision Pro. It’s comfortable for much longer periods of time and not nearly as annoying to actually put on either, as it just feels like putting on a pair of bulky sunglasses. They look a little goofy, obviously, but far less so than a full-on VR headset like any of those mentioned above. This is also the only one of those I consider “mixed reality” thanks to the see-through lenses. Apple and Samsung constantly talk about Vision Pro and Galaxy XR as if they’re mixed reality, but a camera feed is explicitly not true reality. But XREAL’s glasses still aren’t quite just augmented reality, because they’re not just letting you see that digital world through a tiny window, they’re quite literally overlaying everything on top of the real world around you. The illusion is somewhat broken by the limited 70-degree field-of-view and the fact that darker backgrounds often look a little funky when there are light sources in the real world in front of you, but I can say with confidence that this is my favorite version of this experience – the speakers are pretty good too, topping it all off.

    And that brings us to Android XR.

    Recent findings suggest that google’s platform debuted on Samsung’s Galaxy XR headset earlier this year, and it’s all pretty familiar on XREAL Aura. The Android-based experience opens up to a floating launcher of your favorite apps that mostly open up into floating windows in front of you. You can use hand gestures to move everything around or interact with UI elements, and every app I tried worked perfectly well. The gestures can be hit or miss at times, especially the one for going back to the home screen (having this as a long-press that you have to physically look at your hand for gets annoying when doing anything remotely fast-paced, but thankfully the top button is a dedicated home shortcut), but it works well and everything is designed fairly intuitively. A floating cursor demonstrates where you are aiming with a pinch acting as a tap on a touchscreen, and you can move things around in your space as if they’re real objects. There’s a sense of depth throughout the entire experience.

    Some apps open to fully immersive experiences, but these are still in the minority. XREAL touts that there are around 150 experiences launching alongside Aura, but it’s definitely still early days here. Apps like Google TV should obviously be ready for a full format like that but, most things, like the Google Docs app which I’m typing this review in right now, just act as if they’re on independent displays floating around you.

    According to recent reports, like Googlebook, Android XR is also still struggling to figure out the best app experience for each user. Most things are mobile apps, including Google Chrome which is just the standard Android version from your phone. It’s fine in most cases, but I found this restrictive seeing as I can get a ton done in a browser, but fighting mobile optimization is a frustrating way to interact with a window that can be as significant as a TV if you want it to. Meanwhile, the Spotify app is weirdly the web version which is horribly optimized for interacting with hand gestures. I’d have rather had the mobile version here. Another quirk I found was notifications, which pop up at the top of the display and quite literally on top of whatever you’re doing. Something they were invasive, and having to physically reach out to dismiss them is a little annoying. I’m sure there are workflows to help make this less of a distraction, but I’d almost rather have notifications turned off entirely.

    In a recent development, there’s also Gemini, which is core to the experience here. A quick “Hey Google” triggers a Gemini Live session for answering questions, and you can share what you’re seeing to give additional context. It’s way faster than switching between apps to get a quick search done, but there are friction points here, especially if you’re just asking a single question. Gemini answers quickly and leaves the conversation going, great for follow-up queries, bad if you’re done because the UI controls go away, which leaves you to tell Gemini to end the session which, every time, it asks for secondary confirmation you want to end. Google, if I say “end the session,” I think that should be more than sufficient proof I want to end the session. Luckily, a long-press of the top home button fixes that headache, but I still hate that I either need to use a physical control, or basically have to fight an AI to end a conversation that I started hands-free.

    Industry observers note that performance is excellent. Everything is smooth and quick, probably thanks in part to XREAL’s use of 12GB of RAM alongside Qualcomm’s Snapdragon Reality Elite chip.

    But how do you actually use a product like this?

    That’s the question I found myself asking when I first spun up XREAL Aura and started to learn its ins and outs. See, other XREAL glasses have an extremely straightforward use case. Plug in the external device of your choice, get it on a bigger screen. Simple, easy, obvious. I found this helpful in travel primarily, with a bigger display for my MacBook feeling nice for tasks like video editing, while the main value came in just having a very comfortable way to watch a movie on a flight from my connected tablet.

    Both of those use cases are valid on XREAL Aura. You can plug a USB-C device into the puck to get that wired mirroring through an Android XR window, and it works super well. Having Android XR alongside that mirroring also opens the door to added functionality, like having extra windows off to the side for perhaps a media app or reference document if you run out of room on the wired device. As just one example, I kept Spotify and Slack open in side windows while using Aura with my MacBook Air for an afternoon of writing articles.

    I think Android XR makes Aura an absolute powerhouse for media consumption, as you can just download content directly to the device (256GB of storage in the base model) for a flight, or even just use streaming apps if you have Wi-Fi. I couldn’t find any 3D content during my brief review period (nothing in my Google TV library was compatible, apparently), but that’s also on the table. Genuinely, I cannot wait to use these on my next long flight.

    But outside of those, I think a lot of the other scenarios start to fall apart.

    By far the most popular use case for virtual/mixed reality has been gaming. XREAL Aura has a ton of potential here and I’m really excited to try out Project Hail Mary: Journey to the Stars on this, but the fact that these are simply glasses restricts a lot of what you can do. Any major movements could easily result in the glasses slipping or even falling off, whereas a VR headset is much more secure. Stationary immersive gaming has potential, and XREAL’s Gamesir controller collab highlights promise, but I’m just not sold on these as a replacement to something like Meta Quest seeing as the latter already has a deep catalog of games and a much more affordable price.

    Industry observers note that the other use case is productivity, one I’m also not entirely sold on. As mentioned, this entire post was written in Aura, and I’m not sure I benefitted much from that experience versus just using a normal laptop or desktop computer. My workflow was having Google Docs up in the center, typing on a physical keyboard (only a psycho could use the virtual keyboard for anything beyond the shortest messages or passwords) with reference documents in Chrome off to my right and Slack on my left, with the occasional “Hey Google” command helping to find information on the fly (such as the weight comparison earlier). It all works well, but I think Android XR is inherently limited by its reliance mostly on mobile apps, and also just by the use of gestures. You can use a mouse or trackpad, of course, but at that point you might as well just use a laptop.

    XREAL Aura is for a very specific customer from my point of view. Wired mirroring is still very much the strong suit here, with Android XR’s apps and offline video giving these utility outside of just relying on another device. That was my problem with previous XREAL glasses, because the experience just varies wildly depending on what’s connected. Aura’s puck and Android XR experience solves every complaint I had about previous models, while expanding very much on what it can do.

    Sources indicate that further limiting matters is the price. $1,279, in my book, is actually a mostly fair price for this, especially given the RAMageddon of it all. XREAL 1+ Pro come in around $600 and is utterly useless without a secondary device. XREAL Aura more or less doubles the price, but includes the best possible version of that secondary device while also giving you the added camera sensors that are only available as add-ons for other hardware. Don’t get me wrong, it’s still pricey, but I don’t think it’s unfair either, especially not when one of the main competitors for this sort of experience is still $3,600 (which still sounds insane two years later, even for Apple).

    In a recent development, we’ll have far more to say about XREAL Aura in a long-term review from our Nick Sutrich, but the verdict on day one is that Android XR has really solved the biggest problem for XREAL, while XREAL has solved a lot of big problems for Android XR, all while being an overall win for the user at the end of the day. Not so often we get a storybook ending like that in tech anymore, and I’m all here for it.

    According to recent reports, don’t forget, XREAL Aura is $200 off – so $1,099 – through the end of December. Much more worth it at that price.
