    #93349. Tech Report: Power and cooling limits force AI clusters with 100,000+ accelerators to use multiple data centers

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (966 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Tomshardware ↗ Open Full Page

    Tech Report: Power and cooling limits force AI clusters with 100,000+ accelerators to use multiple data centers

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (966 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that the rapid growth of AI clusters is pushing computing infrastructure beyond the physical and power limitations of individual data centers, which creates demand for newly introduced networking architectures capable of connecting compute resources across multiple facilities and even geographical regions.
    • Modern AI clusters typically accommodate more than 100,000 AI accelerators and potentially millions of CPU endpoints, placing tremendous demands on network bandwidth, latency, and congestion management.
    • Recent findings suggest that traditionally, high-performance computing systems have relied on two major interconnect domains: scale-up and scale-out.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that the rapid growth of AI clusters is pushing computing infrastructure beyond the physical and power limitations of individual data centers, which creates demand for newly introduced networking architectures capable of connecting compute resources across multiple facilities and even geographical regions. At Supercomputing 2026 (SC26), researchers from The Ohio State University discussed the evolution of high-performance networking technologies. At the conference, they explained how efficient distributed computing at such a scale requires considerably more than faster network connections, highlighting the importance of scale across domains to stretch workloads across different data centers in separate geographical regions.

    Modern AI clusters typically accommodate more than 100,000 AI accelerators and potentially millions of CPU endpoints, placing tremendous demands on network bandwidth, latency, and congestion management. Meanwhile, an accelerator's computational performance continues to increase faster than communication capabilities, which means that faster AI GPUs do not necessarily deliver proportional improvements in application performance. As a result, the efficiency of network infrastructure determines how effectively large-scale AI systems can use their computational resources.

    Recent findings suggest that traditionally, high-performance computing systems have relied on two major interconnect domains: scale-up and scale-out. Scale-up networks connect processors and accelerators within tightly integrated systems using technologies like AMD's Infinity Fabric, Intel's UPI, Nvidia's NVLink, or emerging alternatives such as UALink. Scale-out networks, which typically rely on Ethernet, InfiniBand, HPE Slingshot, or, more recently, Ultra Ethernet, connect individual servers or rack-scale systems into larger clusters. These interconnects have different requirements for bandwidth, latency, and scalability, which is why they serve different purposes.

    Industry observers note that however, the massive size and power consumption of modern AI clusters create demand for a third interconnect domain, known as scale-across. Unlike scale-out networks, which typically connect systems within a single data center, scale-across architectures extend high-performance connectivity between different buildings, campuses, or even regions.

    Such an approach enables operators to combine computational and other resources from multiple locations to achieve a certain level of performance rather than to bring an excessive number of accelerators to a single data center, which may be hard, or even impossible, due to power availability, cooling requirements, or physical space constraints.

    Industry observers note that the transition toward scale-across architectures has already begun. Google introduced its Virgo network architecture earlier this year to support AI workloads that exceed the space and power capacity of individual data centers. The firm intends to treat an entire campus of computing facilities as a single system, albeit with specialized networks for communication between accelerators, servers, and data centers. Cisco and Marvell are also developing technologies for scale-across deployments, including high-capacity routers, switching chips, and optical interconnects designed to connect geographically distributed clusters.

    In a recent development, extending AI infrastructure beyond individual facilities introduces substantial technical challenges. While modern scale-up networks offer extremely high bandwidth and low latency over relatively short distances, communication between data centers must contend with the physical limitations of long-distance connections. Even optical networks cannot eliminate propagation delays, whereas congestion, packet loss, and synchronization overhead can further reduce effective performance. Consequently, connecting two large GPU clusters with high-speed links does not necessarily make them behave like one tightly integrated computing system.

    According to recent reports, these challenges are particularly key for AI training, where accelerators frequently exchange model parameters, gradients, and intermediate results. Large-scale workloads require efficient collective communications, as delays that affect individual accelerators dramatically reduce the performance of the entire cluster. Therefore, the efficiency of distributed computing depends not only on raw network bandwidth, but also on network topology, congestion management, communication protocols, and software implementations.

    To address these limitations, network adapters and switches are becoming more sophisticated than ever. Modern network interface controllers can perform Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA) operations without continuous CPU involvement, whereas technologies such as HPE Slingshot hardware collectives and Nvidia SHARP can offload certain communication operations to the network infrastructure itself. SmartNICs and data processing units further reduce the burden on host processors as they handle selected network and infrastructure functions in dedicated hardware. Such capabilities can improve efficiency of distributed applications without necessarily requiring faster physical interconnects.

    Recent findings suggest that interestingly, software plays an equally vital role in the performance of large-scale AI infrastructure, as communication frameworks like libfabric, MPI, or UCX determine how applications exchange data and use the capabilities of modern network adapters. Also, GPU-aware communication and technologies like GPUDirect RDMA can eliminate unnecessary transfers through host memory, while optimized collective operations can reduce communication overhead across large numbers of accelerators, according to the researchers.

    The growing complexity of AI infrastructure also changes how operators should evaluate network performance. Although the industry continues to introduce faster interconnect technologies, including versions of GbE with nominal bandwidths of 800 Gb/s and 1.6 Tb/s, peak transfer rates alone do not fully describe the capabilities of a given system because the performance of actual applications depends on multiple factors, including how effectively network hardware and software cooperate to transfer data, prevent congestion, and synchronize computations across thousands of processors.

    According to recent reports, ultimately, the emergence of scale-across interconnection architectures reflects a fundamental change in the design of AI infrastructure. As the computational capabilities of individual accelerators increase and AI clusters expand beyond individual facilities, efficient communication becomes just as important as processor performance. As a result, the next generation of AI systems will depend not only on faster AI accelerators or CPUs, but also on sophisticated network adapters, switches, and, perhaps more importantly, software that can unite geographically distributed computational resources without excessive communication overhead.

    It has been revealed that anton Shilov is a contributing writer at Tom’s Hardware. Over the past couple of decades, he has covered everything from CPUs and GPUs to supercomputers and from modern process technologies and latest fab tools to high-tech industry trends.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Taco Bell is turning up the heat with a new ‘Make It Flamin’ Hot’ customization option that lets customers add spicy Fritos to some of their favorite menu items.

    The fast-food giant has announced a latest limited-time feature that allows customers to upgrade eligible orders with Fritos Flamin’ Hot chips, adding an extra layer of spice and crunch.

    Starting November 24, the customization will be available at participating locations through December 9, giving customers the chance to experiment with some fiery combinations.

    According to Taco Bell’s official announcement, customers can add the chips to popular items including the Crunchwrap Supreme, Cantina Chicken Rolled Quesadilla, and the returning Naked Chicken Chalupa.

    The announcement follows Taco Bell’s recent introduction of the Flamin’ Hot Grilled Cheese Burrito and Flamin’ Hot Mini Taco Salad, the latter of which was first revealed alongside more than 20 new products earlier in 2026.

    “When Taco Bell fans love a menu item, they find ways to make it their own,” remarked Liz Matthews, Taco Bell’s Global Chief Food Innovation Officer.

    “That creativity constantly inspires us, and Make It FLAMIN’ HOT is our way of putting some of that Test Kitchen magic directly into their hands.”.

    Customers can access the latest customization through Taco Bell’s mobile app, website, self-service kiosks, or by ordering at participating restaurants.

    Simply select an eligible menu item, choose the “Customize” or “Modify” option, and add Fritos Flamin’ Hot from the available toppings.

    According to recent reports, however, there are some restrictions. Crunchy tacos, the Cheesy Gordita Crunch, a la carte Nacho Fries, beverages, and desserts are excluded from the promotion.

    Taco Bell puts spicy twist on one of its most popular limited-time items.

    Taco Bell lets fans create & share custom orders in contest to decide next menu item.

    Taco Bell combines two fan-favorite menu items in latest Cantina Chicken Mexican Pizza.

    The spicy upgrade also comes at an additional cost, although Taco Bell has not announced a standard price for the customization.

    The option will also be available through participating third-party delivery services, with prices potentially higher for delivery orders.

    The promotion runs from November 24 through December 9, while supplies last, giving fans just over two weeks to create their own Flamin’ Hot combinations.

If buyers settle from an emailed link and outreach starts late, a reminders tool covers most of it. If customers prefer to pay online by card or ACH, add a payments network with a customer portal. If clients require invoice uploads to Coupa or Ariba and clear multiple invoices with one blank-memo wire, you need an AR automation layer on top of the ERP. Every platform listed here serves B2B businesses invoicing other companies, excluding consumer payment apps and collection agencies.

    Our source material is each vendor's public product, integration, security and pricing pages, plus G2 reviews, as they stood in November 2026.

    Recent findings suggest that about three in five US suppliers let business clients pay within 30 days, per Atradius's 2026 US payment practices survey (September 2026). Most overdue invoices settle within a month past due, so funds arrive roughly two months post-billing. The same survey notes US enterprises often lose 1% to 2% of B2B invoices to bad debt. Software that shortens this window performs four main functions:.

    Sources indicate that what invoice-to-cash software does not handle is core billing operations. Billing schedules, revenue recognition, and GL accounting remain within the ERP. Contract-first platforms initiate workflows from signed agreements and map customer billing prior to collection efforts; invoice-first applications pick up after ERP invoice generation.

    Most finance stacks have four layers: the ERP that creates the invoice and holds the books, a payments network, a reminders tool, and an AR automation layer working the steps in between.

    Recent findings suggest that the ERP covers the last row, and a reminders tool covers timing. The rows in between depend on reading what a customer or a portal sent, which is AR automation work. That share keeps growing. Paper checks fell to 26% of B2B payments in 2025, per the AFP 2025 Digital Payments Survey as reported by Nacha, and FedNow settled about 2.5 times as many payments in Q3 2026 as a year earlier, per Federal Reserve FedNow statistics. Heading into 2027, more money arrives over electronic rails while its remittance detail lands somewhere else.

    On Xero or QuickBooks with customers paying from the emailed link, the leak tends to be timing, and a reminders tool covers it. Once W-9 requests and payment questions fill your team's week, the replies need a different layer.

    It has been revealed that portal rejections and lump-sum wires put the leak in the table's middle rows, where an AR automation layer on the ERP fits. In a demo, we'd ask each vendor to show how fast its software flagged a rejected portal invoice, then to apply a multi-invoice wire with a blank memo live.

    If your team still keys card numbers or chases ACH details, start with the payments layer. A payments network with a customer portal gives buyers stored methods and autopay. Unless the vendor says otherwise, it won't read replies or file into buyer portals, so strategy an AR layer for those stages.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The viral story of a grandmother who accidentally invited a stranger to Thanksgiving dinner is being turned into a Lifetime movie, nearly 10 years after their unlikely friendship began.

    Sources indicate that wanda Dench and Jamal Hinton first made headlines in 2016 when a mistaken text message led to the pair celebrating Thanksgiving together. What started as an accidental invitation has since become an annual tradition, with the two continuing to reunite for the holiday.

    Now, their friendship is heading to television after the pair signed a deal with Lifetime to bring their story to the screen, with a movie expected to arrive in November 2027.

    Dench confirmed to The Arizona Republic on November 16 that she and Hinton recently signed over the rights to their story for a Lifetime movie currently titled ‘The Thanksgiving Grandma.’.

    The film is expected to begin production in early 2027, with producer Jack Leslie targeting a November release that same year.

    “They did tell us right up front that it’s based on our story,” Dench explained.

    Hinton also unveiled the news on Instagram, sharing a photo alongside Dench and celebrating their partnership with Lifetime.

    “Very excited to officially be in business with Lifetime!” he wrote. “They believe in our story, and it truly feels like we’re in the best hands as we take this next step.”.

    He also thanked Dench for being a constant source of support throughout their friendship, telling followers that their journey was only getting started.

    The pair’s story began in November 2016 when Dench accidentally texted Hinton while attempting to invite her grandson to Thanksgiving dinner. Unbeknownst to her, her grandson had changed his phone number, and Hinton received the invitation instead.

    Viral couple responds after actress secretly records them getting engaged.

    According to recent reports, after exchanging messages and photos, the two realized they were strangers. However, Hinton jokingly asked whether he could still attend dinner.

    “Of course you can, that’s what grandmas do … feed everyone,” Dench responded.

    Their exchange quickly went viral on Twitter, and Hinton ultimately joined Dench and her family for Thanksgiving at her home in Arizona.

    The tradition has continued every year since, with the pair sharing updates about their friendship on social media.

    The upcoming Lifetime movie has been in development in various forms for years. Leslie initially approached Dench about adapting the story in 2018 while working at Netflix, but the project was eventually abandoned following downsizing at the tech giant.

    Screenwriter Glen Dolman is now working on the Lifetime adaptation and recently spent a weekend at Dench’s home to learn more about their relationship.

    “It’s going to be more of how we’ve supported each other throughout the 10 years,” Dench explained.

    • Google Voice is a wonderful service that’s often neglected, but with RCS supposedly on the way, a fresh app redesign is now rolling out on Android that might as well have a substantial neon sign that claims “RCS is coming.”.
    • Google Voice is a US-only service that operates a phone number over the internet.
    • That might finally be changing, though.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Google Voice is a wonderful service that’s often neglected, but with RCS supposedly on the way, a fresh app redesign is now rolling out on Android that might as well have a substantial neon sign that claims “RCS is coming.”.

    Google Voice is a US-only service that operates a phone number over the internet. No normal carrier, just an app tied to your Google account that gets a phone number with the ability to make calls and send/receive text messages. The latter, though, has been a point of contention for the past few years as Voice was excluded from Google’s huge push into RCS.

    That might finally be changing, though. Recent updates brought mention of RCS in the app’s code.

    Now, a slightly newer version (v2026-11-01-1019342246) of Google Voice has debuted a redesign for the app on Android.

    The upcoming look isn’t a drastic restructuring, but a huge coat of paint on an app that hasn’t seen any meaningful updates since 2023. The new look feels more modern and very much influenced by Google Messages. The text field at the bottom has a rounded design with the same “+” and camera icons found in Messages, as well as a new long-press gesture that is, again, similar to Google’s primary messaging app. The main page hasn’t been updated beyond a new, rounded search bar up top and some subtly bolder fonts.

    Material You colors are hit or miss now. On a Pixel with an orange theme, that color influenced the entire UI, but on a Galaxy Z Fold 8 with a coral/blue theme, the only sign of themeing was a blue message field.

    In a recent development, the most notable thing here is the “SMS” icon on the send button, which looks just like the button in Google Messages. In that app, it’s used as an indicator as to what type of message you’re sending – SMS or RCS. Combined with code in that other recent patch directly pointing to “RCS” being used on a send button, you can absolutely tell Google Voice is finally adding this long-overdue functionality.

    A timeline for RCS support in Google Voice is still unclear, but this redesign going live now certainly suggests it’s coming sooner rather than later.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The smart glasses race is heating up as Meta and Samsung are about to go head-to-head, but could a new Meta glasses style fix the privacy stigma, or are things too far gone?

    In a recent development, meta released its own-branded smart glasses this summer (read: with no Ray-Ban or Oakley branding), and they seem to have done well for a number of reasons. Some models are much cheaper than Ray-Ban-branded pairs, while other Meta glasses carry Kylie Jenner or LISA names, bringing in a unique note of fashion, but none of these models changed the look of the camera LED indicator on the front.

    According to recent reports, meta has come under fire over the past two years as people have abused the company’s smart glasses, giving them the unfortunate term “perv glasses” on social media because some people disabled the camera LED, which is supposed to illuminate when the camera is recording. Meta has issued several different software patches to disable the glasses’ camera when the LED is tampered with, but many have begun to feel like having a camera on smart glasses just feels wrong after people have abused the technology.

    Meta glasses product lead David Woodland posted a render of the Gentle Monster cateye style glasses in a now-deleted Tweet on X on November 17, simply saying “I plead the fifth.” Presumably, he was calling out how similar these glasses look to the Meta Starfire Kylie Jenner style, but we’ll likely never know now.

    Samsung and Google’s Warby Parker and Gentle Monster glasses certainly resemble Meta’s glasses, but they also do something noticeably different: the camera LED doesn’t look like the camera on the other side.

    Recent findings suggest that so this begs the question: can Meta do anything to salvage the unsavory association its glasses now have attached to them? We covered this topic on episode 125 of our Pixelated podcast, and Woodland’s post further highlights the question. A camera LED that’s obviously different from the camera on the other side would likely prompt people to ask about your glasses, while Meta’s design is purposefully stealthy because of its symmetry.

    Does this design difference help Samsung’s Gentle Monster/Warby Parker glasses feel more private, and would a similar redesign help Meta’s glasses? I think it would help a lot, but I also want to know what our readers think. What say you, folks?

    Best Ecommerce Platforms for Developers: Six Options and the Layers Each Leaves to You

    📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (735 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sitepoint

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.
    • According to recent reports, picking an ecommerce platform is really a decision about which layers you want to own: the storefront, the catalog and order logic, the payment flow, and the hosting underneath.
    • In a recent development, shopify is the fully managed option.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

    Weekly. Free. One click to leave.

    7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

    According to recent reports, picking an ecommerce platform is really a decision about which layers you want to own: the storefront, the catalog and order logic, the payment flow, and the hosting underneath. Every platform below draws that line in a different place. If you have already settled the front-end question with a comparison like SitePoint's Astro vs Next.js guide, the next question is what sits behind it. Prices are from each vendor's pricing page as of November 2026.

    In a recent development, shopify is the fully managed option. Basic costs $29 a month with card rates from 2.9% plus 30 cents, and a 2% fee applies to orders processed through a third-party gateway on that plan. Developers get two routes: Liquid themes, or Hydrogen, Shopify's headless toolkit, where your framework owns routing and rendering and Hydrogen supplies the Storefront API client and cart. Templates exist for React Router on Oxygen and for Next.js on Vercel. Plus starts at $2,300 a month.

    It has been revealed that whop is a business platform for taking payments and sending payouts, and it sits under a storefront you have already built rather than replacing it. The Checkout element runs in the browser with no server code and no API key on the page. You pass your own order ID as metadata, Whop copies it onto the payment, and your server fulfills from a signed webhook that follows the Standard Webhooks spec. Domestic cards cost 2.7% plus 30 cents with no monthly fee, buyers see payment methods chosen by their location across 195 countries, and the same balance pays out in over 200 countries, including to affiliates or sellers you onboard. Whop's own guide highlights how to integrate a checkout API into a Next.js storefront end to end. The trade-off is that there is no catalog or shipping engine; you collect address fields at checkout and trigger fulfillment from the webhook.

    WooCommerce is a free plugin on WordPress you host yourself, so you own updates, security, and performance. Its payment gateway, WooPayments, charges US merchants 2.9% plus 30 cents per card transaction, 1.5% more for international cards, 2% for currency conversion, and $25 per dispute. Everything is PHP hooks and filters, which makes it the natural pick for agencies already living in WordPress and the wrong pick for anyone who does not want to run a server.

    BigCommerce hosts the back end and lets you bring any front end. Core is $29 a month billed annually, capped at $30,000 in trailing annual sales, and plans auto-upgrade as volume grows. There are no platform fees when you use an embedded payment provider, and a 2% fee on Core if you use another one. Catalyst, its reference storefront, is built on Next.js, React Server Components, and the Storefront GraphQL API, and deploys to Vercel.

    In a recent development, medusa is an open-source commerce framework in Node.js and TypeScript, with an MIT-licensed core and a commercial enterprise edition. SitePoint covered it when it was still a young Shopify alternative; it now has over 37,000 GitHub stars. Self-hosting is free. Medusa Cloud starts at $29 a month for development, $99 for launch, and $299 for scale, with no percentage of sales, and the firm claims you can export your data and self-host at any point.

    Saleor is a GraphQL-native, API-only commerce platform written in Python and released under the BSD-3 license. Self-hosting is free. Saleor Cloud starts at $1,599 a month for up to $200,000 in monthly sales, with 0.8% on orders above that, and $3,999 a month at the next tier. It is built for teams with a dedicated engineering function and a large catalog, which is exactly who should pay that price.

    It has been revealed that own only the storefront, and Shopify or BigCommerce will carry the rest. Own everything, and Medusa or Saleor give you a back end you can read. Already on WordPress, and WooCommerce is the obvious fit. Already have a storefront in Next.js or Astro and only need the money to move, and Whop is the shortest path. Whichever you pick, the checkout is where disputes start, so log what SitePoint's friendly fraud guide for developers recommends from day one.

    #93329. MSI EdgeMesa N AI+ review: RTX Spark power comes to Windows on Arm desktops, but there are trade-offs

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 17m • 📚 Deep Dive (3384 w)

    MSI EdgeMesa N AI+ review: RTX Spark power comes to Windows on Arm desktops, but there are trade-offs

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3384 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

    ⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that MSI's EdgeMesa N AI+ mini PC brings Nvidia RTX Spark power to a Windows on Arm desktop.
    • Solid local AI performance for LLMs and image generation, as expected.
    • Familiar Windows 11 user experience and app compatibility.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that MSI's EdgeMesa N AI+ mini PC brings Nvidia RTX Spark power to a Windows on Arm desktop. It offers broad app compatibility and the same strong local AI performance we've come to expect from Nvidia's GB10 SoC, but it's still very expensive and less expandable than DGX Spark systems.

    Solid local AI performance for LLMs and image generation, as expected.

    Familiar Windows 11 user experience and app compatibility.

    Could use more peripheral I/O and smarter port placement.

    Loses the DGX Spark's clustering capability.

    Getting the best gaming performance requires patience.

    It has been revealed that why you can trust Tom's Hardware Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

    It has been revealed that nvidia’s RTX Spark platform, powered by the RTX Spark N1X SoC, passed its most difficult test yet last month at the heart of Windows on Arm laptops. Now we get to see how that chip serves as a Windows on Arm foundation for compact desktops.

    We’ve got our hands on the MSI EdgeMesa N AI+, a $7,500 RTX Spark mini PC that gives Windows-native creators and local AI trailblazers access to the same powerful 6144-core Blackwell GPU and 20-core Arm CPU that we recently put to the test in the Surface Laptop Ultra, along with a 128GB pool of unified memory and 4TB of storage in our tested config.

    We’ve been testing Nvidia GB10-powered desktop systems for almost a year now in the form of the DGX Spark and friends, and the EdgeMesa N AI+’s design is typical of the breed. It’s wrapped in a slightly hollow-feeling matte aluminum shell with shiny diamond-cut edges and a white plastic back plate.

    In a recent development, the design and build quality of this system is a tad underwhelming for the price. It feels nice enough, but It’s hardly a precision-milled statement piece for your desk like a Mac Mini or Mac Studio.

    Industry observers note that the EdgeMesa draws cool air in through its perforated front panel, which then passes through a dual-fan heatsink with a vapor-chamber base and exhausts through the back panel. The rounded rectangle on the top half of the front panel might look like an optical drive tray, but it’s a purely cosmetic accent.

    It has been revealed that around back, the EdgeMesa comes equipped with a 10 Gigabit Ethernet jack, an HDMI 2.1 port, and three USB Type-C 20 Gbps ports with DisplayPort Alt Mode support. A fourth USB-C port is dedicated to the system’s 240 W USB-PD power adapter. The EdgeMesa also has Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 5.4 radios inside.

    Industry observers note that even with a wireless keyboard and mouse, three 20Gbps USB-C ports feel a bit skimpy as the sole expansion options on a $7,499 PC that’s positioned as a do-it-all desktop for content creation and gaming. If you need to connect multiple monitors to an RTX Spark via USB-C, those scant options for peripheral connectivity shrink even further.

    Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

    Industry observers note that for comparison, a similarly priced Mac Studio gives you four 80Gbps Thunderbolt 5 ports around back and two more USB Type-C ports, plus an SD card reader, up front. The Mac even provides a headphone jack, while the EdgeMesa requires you to plug in a USB headset or DAC or pair Bluetooth earbuds for audio output.

    Even the Mac Mini gives you three Thunderbolt ports out back and two USB 3 10Gbps ports out front.

    In use, the tightly spaced, rear-mounted USB-C ports make for an annoying time when doing frequent unplugging and replugging of devices like card readers and external SSDs that are typical in creative workflows. Even one front-panel USB-C port would have made a huge difference in the ease of use of this design.

    Industry observers note that the EdgeMesa also drops the handy ConnectX RDMA NIC that lets you cluster DGX Spark systems together to run larger AI models. That omission raises a weighty question: is Windows support and application compatibility important enough to trade away any chance of expanding your local AI foundation in the future?

    Having tested DGX Sparks for some time now, I’m not sure that’s a wise trade-off, given that most anybody reading this already has a capable Windows PC or Mac that can link up with a DGX Spark for many local AI compute jobs using the Nvidia Sync app.

    DGX Spark prices are rising, but you can get MSI's own EdgeXpert with 128GB of memory and a 4TB SSD on sale for $8,099 right now (or $8,499 at full price). Even a $1000 difference in price for that ConnectX NIC in this rarefied air of PC pricing would give me pause if I'm seriously considering how to add local AI capacity to my home.

    Recent findings suggest that if you have no inclination whatsoever to learn Linux or networking concepts and just want a no-questions-asked, AI-capable Windows mini PC that can serve as your primary desktop, an RTX Spark system like this may be the way to go. But you'll want to be really sure of your decision before dropping this much cash.

    20-core Arm CPU (10 X925 performance cores, 10 A725 efficiency cores).

    6144-core (48 SM) Nvidia Blackwell integrated GPU.

    128GB LPDDR5X, 273 GB/s shared memory bandwidth.

    10 Gigabit Ethernet, Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 5.4.

    3x USB 3.2 Gen 2x2 Type-C ports (rear).

    The performance of the Nvidia GB10 SoC's CPU and GPU resources, whether under DGX OS or Windows, is well-trodden ground by this point. But for a fresh point of comparison, we grabbed AMD’s Ryzen AI Halo, swapped in a spare SSD, and installed Windows 11 Pro, as the Ryzen AI Halo is the only other Windows-ready platform with a large unified memory pool for AI adventurers.

    Industry observers note that in the Geekbench 7 CPU benchmark under Windows, the Ryzen AI Halo delivers a slightly higher single-threaded score than the MSI EdgeMesa’s RTX Spark Superchip, but its multithreaded score trails the Nvidia part. Using Linux, we would expect both scores to be higher for the Ryzen CPU. But the broader point remains the same: you can expect similar performance from both of these CPUs under Windows.

    Recent findings suggest that we’ve left Apple’s Mac Studio with M4 Max in these charts just to emphasize the large performance lead Apple Silicon holds in this benchmark, even with older chips. The current M5 Max would likely open an even larger lead.

    In the AgentPerf-Local AI inference benchmark, the MSI EdgeMesa delivered performance practically identical to Microsoft’s Surface Laptop Ultra when running the same Qwen 3.8 27B model with DFlash2 speculative decoding. Its desktop form factor doesn’t seem to give it any extra performance headroom, at least for this LLM serving configuration. Other workloads or models could reveal a difference.

    It has been revealed that we already tested the RTX Spark against the Ryzen AI Halo in AgentPerf-Local in our Surface Laptop Ultra review, and AMD’s platform ended up way behind GB10 in those tests. And in this newly introduced round of testing, AMD's LLM performance is worse under Windows with the Vulkan backend than in Linux with ROCm, taking a whopping four times as long as the EdgeMesa to complete the benchmark.

    Strix Halo might have been an appealing local inference option when it was the only open and relatively hackable unified memory platform around, but if you’re serious about local AI performance (and especially if tokens equal dollars for you), a GB10 system is the superior choice in late 2026.

    Gaming on RTX Spark continues to be a bit of a weird time, and the MSI EdgeMesa N doesn’t change that experience, even with a more generous power and thermal budget than the Surface Laptop Ultra I've already tested.

    Sources indicate that this platform just doesn’t respond to tuning as we might expect from our experience with traditional gaming PCs and laptops. That weirdness stems, in part, from the imbalance between memory bandwidth and compute resources on GB10.

    The 48 SMs of the RTX Spark N1X GPU have to share just 273 GB/s of LPDDR5X bandwidth with the CPU. Compare that with the 672 GB/s of dedicated bandwidth the similarly-specced RTX 5070 enjoys from its 12 GB of GDDR7.

    Architectural decisions aside, the RTX Spark platform's gaming performance isn't helped by the fact that full GPU utilization is seemingly hampered by the overhead of Prism x86 emulation in most games. Few (if any) major titles have Arm ports, so this is just a fact of life for the foreseeable future if you buy one of these systems.

    Let's see how this all plays out in practice for the RTX Spark versus the Radeon 8060S on board AMD's Strix Halo.

    Sources indicate that in the 3DMark Steel Nomad raster benchmark, the RTX Spark holds a wide lead over the Ryzen AI Halo, delivering a roughly 56% higher score. That result would suggest a knockout in games for Nvidia’s platform.

    Industry observers note that but Steel Nomad isn’t representative of real-world gaming performance on the RTX Spark. If we fire up Control Resonant on both platforms and choose the High raster preset at 1440p with Performance upscaling (a 1280x720 input resolution), the RTX Spark and Strix Halo end up a lot closer.

    Recent findings suggest that notably, though, the RTX Spark desktop delivers considerably worse 1% low FPS performance than the Ryzen AI Halo, and this does manifest as visible stutter and hitching. So it's not a clear win for the Nvidia platform.

    AMD fans might take heart in the fact that Strix Halo can get this close to the RTX Spark on this raster gaming baseline, but the Radeon 8060S doesn’t have nearly as many tricks up its sleeve to further juice performance.

    Recent findings suggest that for one, the quality of FSR 4 upscaling at lower input resolutions on RDNA 3.5 is still not up to par with what you can get out of DLSS 4.5. For two, the Radeon 8060S’s RDNA 3.5 CUs don't match up well against the Spark's Blackwell-powered RT chops.

    And FSR Frame Generation is still limited to a doubling of a base frame rate, so you can’t smooth out gameplay on a high-refresh-rate monitor nearly as well as you can with DLSS MFG.

    So even if their raster baseline frame rates are similar, the Radeon 8060S isn't delivering the same image quality in Control Resonant as an RTX Spark system does with all its DLSS features in play.

    In a recent development, RT is the next step for squeezing better image quality out of Control Resonant. Surprisingly, enabling RT Medium only results in a 14% performance hit on the Spark versus 38% on the AI Halo. That might be due in part to the efficiency of DLSS Ray Reconstruction versus the Northlight engine's built-in denoiser, but the RT prowess of Blackwell certainly can't hurt.

    A 52.3 FPS average with a 75 ms average PC latency is an OK baseline — at least in the context of an RTX Spark system — for adding MFG to the mix for a smoother experience, especially since Control Resonant seems to link Nvidia Reflex latency reduction to that tech anyway. But dialing in MFG 3X with the default MFG Preset B model still results in a PC latency of 96 ms on average, which is too high to be enjoyable, even if we give the Spark some slack.

    Sources indicate that I found that the new MFG Preset C, available through the Nvidia App, significantly lowered latency versus the more compute-intensive Preset B. While input latency with Preset C is still high at about 84 ms, we have to take every bit of help we can get here, and the resulting 145 FPS average is notably smoother than native gameplay on my 160 Hz monitor.

    We only had time to dive into this one title in our testing, but when Nvidia claims the RTX Spark platform is great for 1440p gaming, our experience suggests that you need to be ready to tweak DLSS upscaling and dial in MFG for more demanding games. And look: that’s fine. These are proven technologies at this point, and they let us get a better experience out of this platform than native rendering would allow.

    But all of these data points should go to show that if you're used to the low input latency and predictable performance scaling characteristics of an x86 desktop gaming PC with a discrete GPU, the RTX Spark platform still has a ways to go before it can truly replace such a system.

    During our AgentPerf-Local LLM benchmark, the EdgeMesa N AI+ pulls about 140 W from the wall, and under that load, it produces just 38.2 dBA at 18” (46 cm) according to our calibrated SPL meter, well below the 47.4 dBA of the RTX Spark-powered Surface Laptop Ultra and the 48 dBA of the Ryzen AI Halo.

    That makes the EdgeMesa an easy system to live with for local AI work, especially if it’s moonlighting as an AI inference server or always-on agent host in shared spaces.

    Under gaming workloads, the EdgeMesa draws about 200 W. With more heat to dissipate, the MSI box’s noise output rises to 40.7 dBA, which is still much quieter than the average gaming laptop and will easily be covered by speakers or a closed-back gaming headset.

    The Ryzen AI Halo, on the other hand, emits a piercing 46.9 dBA whine while gaming, much closer to what we expect from a gaming laptop. And that’s not because it has that much more heat to dissipate; the AI Halo is pulling about 209 W with Control Resonant running.

    In a recent development, under that same load, the EdgeMesa’s fans have a slightly high-pitched character to them, but it’s much less pronounced than the typical gaming laptop. Mostly, the sound from the system is that of air moving, and it's easy to ignore (so much so that I missed the aural cues I sometimes listen for when a benchmark finishes).

    MSI deserves high praise for this system’s thermal design and cooling system. It’s both quiet and pleasant-sounding, and those factors aren’t always a given with mini PCs.

    If you’re a hardcore Windows fan who’s been intrigued by Nvidia’s DGX Sparks for local AI, but you've been repelled by the idea of using Linux, RTX Spark desktops like this MSI EdgeMesa N AI+ finally pair your preferred OS with the same 6144-core Nvidia Blackwell GPU, 20-core Arm CPU, and up to 128GB of unified memory that give those systems their local AI grunt.

    These systems are a potentially exciting prospect for those who want to explore the possibilities of local AI and agentic workflows without the privacy and token caps of cloud models, all from the comfort of Windows.

    In a recent development, but that potential comes with tradeoffs that you’ll need to weigh carefully before buying. And at an eye-popping $7,499 for the 128GB EdgeMesa configuration with a 4TB SSD that we tested, those tradeoffs weigh all the more heavily.

    The MSI EdgeMesa N AI+ delivers essentially the same performance from the RTX Spark N1X SoC (aka GB10) we’ve come to know and love for about a year now. It’s reasonably fast for local LLM inference, and it offers leading performance with generative AI workflows like images and videos in ComfyUI. Its Arm CPU offers solid enough single-threaded and multi-threaded performance for general computing tasks, and it can game in a pinch. The EdgeMesa is laudably quiet, too — no small feat for a compact PC like this.

    Recent findings suggest that but in exchange for Windows support, RTX Spark desktops lose the valuable expandability offered by the ConnectX 7 RDMA NIC that comes standard on DGX Spark boxes. So if you want to try your hand at running a bigger, more intelligent LLM than you can fit in one of these systems’ unified memory pools through clustering, you are forever out of luck if you go down the RTX path.

    Even if you can live without the ConnectX NIC, we’re a bit let down by the peripheral connectivity the EdgeMesa N AI+ offers, both for its price and for its ambitions as a do-it-all creator and gaming system.

    Recent findings suggest that with just three 20 Gbps USB Type-C ports on the back panel that have to do double duty as display outputs in multi-monitor setups, folks who have to juggle external storage and card readers frequently may find both the number and placement of those ports an obstacle to a smooth workflow. We really would have liked to see more expansion ports on this system overall, or at least one on the front panel.

    Nvidia loves to tout the gaming capability of Windows on Arm with RTX Spark systems, but we're still not that impressed by the experience in practice, especially for a system this expensive.

    Industry observers note that it's nice that you can enjoy PC gaming on these systems at all, but even in a desktop with more power and thermal budget to spare, the gaming performance and responsiveness we saw can only be described as adequate. We were especially surprised by the gulf in 1% low FPS between the RTX Spark and the much cheaper Ryzen AI Halo in Control Resonant, despite the RTX Spark N1X's much stronger GPU on paper.

    Recent findings suggest that in general, we find that it takes a lot of careful tweaking and application of DLSS magic to get around this platform's wrinkles for gaming (or a willingness to just let the Nvidia App optimize your game settings). In other words, don't retire your dedicated gaming PC or laptop just yet.

    The large memory pools available from RTX Spark systems have uses beyond local AI, of course. Nvidia GPUs are favorites for creative work on Windows, and if you work with massive 3D or game development projects, or you edit lots of high-resolution video, RTX Sparks are the first unified memory systems to pair a powerful Nvidia GPU with this much VRAM for Windows consumers.

    Adobe just updated several of its Creative Suite apps with Arm-native versions, so if you’re trying to blaze the trail of agentic content creation and generation in this modern age, an RTX Spark desktop (or laptop, for that matter) might be intriguing.

    But we feel like $7,499 is still a ton of money to spend on a system like this to run Adobe's apps specifically, unless a large unified memory pool is particularly useful for your work today.

    According to recent reports, all told, we're left scratching our heads a bit about who RTX Spark desktops are really for. RTX Spark laptops meaningfully expanded the capabilities of mobile Windows on Arm systems thanks to the unmatched AI compute resources of their Blackwell GPUs and support for the full Nvidia software stack, along with solid CPU performance and battery life.

    But compared to both the existing DGX Spark platform and other mini PCs, RTX Spark desktops like the MSI EdgeMesa N AI+ ask you to give up a lot in exchange for the Nvidia-powered Windows on Arm experience, especially for the high prices they’re likely to command amid the current silicon supply crunch.

    If you’re a hardcore Windows-native developer or creator looking to explore the boundaries of what’s possible from local and agentic AI and want the best possible Microsoft-powered foundation for those activities, an RTX Spark desktop might be the right choice for the job, assuming you have the cash.

    But if you're just curious, we'd wait for the value proposition of local or agentic AI under Windows to firm up a bit and for the prices of these systems to come down before spending thousands of dollars on a still-fuzzy vision of the future of computing.

    It has been revealed that as the Senior Analyst, Graphics at Tom's Hardware, Jeff Kampman covers everything that has to do with graphics cards, gaming performance, and more. From integrated graphics processors to discrete graphics cards to the hyperscale installations powering our AI future, if it's got a GPU in it, Jeff is on it.

    Jimmy John’s is celebrating the holiday season with a limited-time meal inspired by National Lampoon’s Christmas Vacation, featuring newly introduced menu items and exclusive collectibles based on the classic comedy.

    Industry observers note that the sandwich chain has partnered with Warner Bros. to launch the Christmas Vacation Feast, bringing several references from the 1989 holiday film to its restaurants nationwide.

    Beginning November 23, customers can order the themed meal at participating Jimmy John’s locations, with the promotion also extending beyond the menu through exclusive merchandise and a holiday-themed restaurant makeover in Chicago.

    The Christmas Vacation Feast features three holiday-inspired menu items, custom packaging based on the movie, and a collectible turtleneck dickie inspired by Cousin Eddie.

    A post shared by Markie_devo (@markie_devo).

    Those interested in collecting all four Cousin Eddie-inspired dickies will be able to purchase them individually without ordering the complete meal.

    “When it comes to the holidays, Clark Griswold set the bar impossibly high,” said Suzanne DeRouchie, Vice President of Integrated Marketing Communications at Jimmy John’s.

    “We wanted to capture that same over-the-top energy in a way only Jimmy John’s could. From festive new menu items to the Cousin Eddie-inspired dickie, the Christmas Vacation Feast gives fans a delicious excuse to lean into a little holiday chaos.”.

    Jimmy John’s is also transforming its restaurant at 501 N. LaSalle Drive in Chicago with 25,000 holiday lights, recreating one of the film’s most recognizable scenes.

    The decorated restaurant will be on display from November 21 through December 26, paying tribute to the movie’s Chicago-area setting and the sandwich chain’s origins.

    Burger King unveils Snoopy meals for adults and kids with exclusive Peanuts collectibles.

    Jimmy John’s is giving away free Picklewiches to customers who dress as pickles.

    McDonald’s reveals Home Alone Meal with pizza-flavored fries and collectible socks.

    Additionally, a limited-edition merchandise collection will launch November 23 through the Jimmy Store, featuring a squirrel plushie, a Clark Griswold-inspired hockey jersey, and a Cousin Eddie-inspired trapper hat.

    Jimmy John’s is the latest fast food chain to embrace holiday nostalgia, following McDonald’s Home Alone Meal, which features pizza-flavored fries and collectible socks, and Burger King’s Peanuts collaboration, which includes Snoopy-themed meals for adults and kids alongside exclusive holiday collectibles.

    #93324. What is Model Routing in AI?

    📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1980 w)

    What is Model Routing in AI?

    📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1980 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sitepoint

    ⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.
    • According to recent reports, weekly.
    • In a recent development, 7 Day Free Trial.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

    According to recent reports, weekly. Free. One click to leave.

    In a recent development, 7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

    Sources indicate that "Do you know the closest ATM?" and "I was charged twice, the refund never arrived, and now my card is blocked" are both customer messages. Most AI apps send both to the same large model and pay large-model prices for each one.

    Model routing fixes that. A router looks at each request and sends it to the cheapest model that can handle it, and keeps the expensive model for the requests that need it.

    Sources indicate that in this guide we'll cover what model routing is, how routers decide, and what it saves. Then we'll build a small router in about 60 lines of JavaScript and run it over 200 customer messages. At one setting it matched a large model's accuracy for about a third of the cost. At another it came within a point and a half for 89% less.

    Model routing in AI is the practice of sending each request to the model best suited to it, instead of sending every request to one model. A router sits between your app and a pool of models, reads each request, and picks a model based on what you care about: cost, speed, or quality.

    You'll also see it called AI model routing, LLM routing, or LLM model routing. They all mean the same thing. The pool might be a small and a large model from one provider, or models from several providers behind one API.

    The idea rests on one observation: most requests are easy. A small model answers them as well as a large one, in a fraction of the time and for a fraction of the price. The router's whole job is finding the hard ones.

    The diagram below shows a typical AI model routing architecture.

    Model routing works in three steps: the router reads the request, decides which model should answer it, and forwards the request to that model. The middle step is where routers differ. Routing tools decide which model to use in one of four ways.

    Industry observers note that rule-based routing uses rules you write by hand. Requests from free-plan users go to a small model. Anything tagged as code goes to a coding model. Prompts over a certain length go to a model with a bigger context window. It's simple, predictable, and free to run, but the rules only know what you thought of in advance.

    Industry observers note that intelligent model routing uses a model to make the decision. A small, fast classifier reads each request and predicts which model in the pool will answer it well. You'll also see it called smart or dynamic model routing.

    Sources indicate that two more terms come up here. Task-aware routing picks a model by the kind of job, like summarising, coding, or answering a support question. Context-aware routing also looks at what surrounds the request, like the conversation so far, the user, or the tools available.

    Sources indicate that the significant platforms work this way. Microsoft describes its Foundry model router as "a trained language model" that picks a model for each prompt in real time. Google states Gemini Notebook uses its new Decisions API as a real-time router, serving everyday queries with up to 40% lower latency. I've tested the Google Decisions API against Jev on the same messages we'll use below.

    Sources indicate that cascade routing tries the cheapest model first and only moves up when the answer isn't good enough. The usual test is confidence: if the cheap model is sure, keep its answer. If it isn't, send the request to a stronger model. It's also called confidence-based routing, and it's what we'll build below.

    It has been revealed that A cascade needs no separate classifier, because the first model's own confidence does the routing. The trade-off is that escalated requests pay for two models and wait for both.

    It has been revealed that fallback routing is about staying up, not saving money. If a model times out, hits a rate limit, or its provider has an outage, the router sends the request to the next model on a list. Most production routers combine fallbacks with one of the three methods above.

    The main benefits of model routing in AI systems are lower cost, faster responses, and fewer outages, without giving up quality on the hard requests.

    In a recent development, we'll build a cascade router for a job every support tool has: sorting customer messages. Each message gets one of ten labels, like atm support or request refund.

    The test set is 200 messages from Banking77, a public set of banking support messages: ten labels, 20 messages each. They're the same 200 messages from my zero shot classification test, which is where the single-model numbers below come from.

    Sources indicate that put both keys in a .env file and run the examples with node --env-file=.env. It's the same setup as in my guide to getting a YouTube API key.

    Sources indicate that create router.mjs. The first function sends the message to Jev with one multiple-choice question, and returns the label Jev picked along with its confidence:.

    In a recent development, confidence runs from 0 to 1. When nearly all the probability sits on one label, it's close to 1. When Jev is torn between two labels, it drops.

    It has been revealed that the second function asks Claude Opus 5.5 the same question. The output_config block limits the answer to one of our labels, so there's no free text to parse. SitePoint's guide to LLM structured output with JSON Schema explains how that works.

    The router itself is about a dozen lines:.

    According to recent reports, if Jev is at least 80% confident, its answer goes straight back. If not, Claude answers instead. And if Claude fails, the router falls back to Jev's answer, because a shaky answer beats an error page.

    Try it on an easy message and a harder one:.

    According to recent reports, jev was sure about the lost card. On the ATM question it leaned towards card acceptance with a confidence of 0.64, so the router asked Claude, which got it right.

    Because cheap, strong, and threshold are options, the same function routes between any two models.

    Model routing reduces AI costs by keeping easy requests on a cheap model and paying for the expensive one only when it's needed. Here's what that looked like on our 200 messages, starting with each model on its own:.

    Opus gets six more messages right out of 200, and costs more than 120 times as much.

    Now the router, at four confidence thresholds:.

    Industry observers note that speed improved too. At the 0.8 threshold, the messages Jev kept came back in a median of 227 ms. The ones that escalated took about 2.1 seconds, because they waited for both models.

    A note on method: I ran every message through both models once and saved the answers, then replayed the router over them at each threshold. That's how you compare thresholds without paying for the same test four times.

    Industry observers note that then I ran the router live to check. At 0.95 it scored the same 95.0% and sent 61 messages to Opus. At 0.8 it scored 93.5% and sent 20, a point under the replay. Two answers moved: one of Jev's confidence scores landed at 0.82 instead of 0.78, just over the line, and Opus changed its answer on one message. Scores near the threshold shift a little between runs, so leave yourself a margin.

    Industry observers note that the choice of cheap model matters less than you'd think. With Google's Gemini Decision 1 in first place instead of Jev, a 0.7 threshold reached the same 95% for US$0.28 per 1,000 messages.

    Recent findings suggest that model routing can cost a little quality, and the threshold decides how much. In our test the gap to Opus ranged from nothing at 0.95 to two points at 0.7.

    The loss comes from one place: answers the cheap model got wrong while feeling sure. At the 0.8 threshold, Jev kept five wrong answers because its confidence was above the line. Opus got four of those five wrong as well, so only one was a real loss: "Do all ATMs take this card?", which Jev filed under card acceptance with a confidence of 0.91.

    Sources indicate that escalating isn't risk-free either. On one message, Jev had the right label with a confidence of 0.44, and Opus overruled it with the wrong one.

    To optimize costs using AI model routing, measure first, route second, and keep measuring. These six steps cover LLM model routing cost optimization for any pair of models:.

    Recent findings suggest that the return is easy to estimate once you know the split. If nine in ten requests stay on a model that costs 1% as much, the bill drops by about 89%, which is what we measured.

    Sources indicate that several inference providers have multi-model routing built in, and most AI gateway platforms support model routing too, so you don't have to write your own. As of November 2026, these are the top model routing solutions for AI apps. Each name links to the tool's model routing docs:.

    Hosted model routing platforms for large language models decide for you, which is the fastest way to start. A hand-built router like ours takes more work, but you choose the signal and you can see why every request went where it did.

    An LLM router is the component that does model routing for large language models. It can be a function in your own code, like the one in this guide, a hosted model such as Microsoft Foundry's model router, or a feature of an AI gateway.

    In a recent development, smart model routing is another name for intelligent model routing: a model, not a hand-written rule, decides where each request goes. Dynamic model routing means the same thing.

    The ROI of AI model routing depends on how much of your traffic a cheaper model can handle. In our test, a 0.8 threshold kept 89.5% of messages on the cheap model and cut the cost per 1,000 messages from US$1.96 to US$0.22, for about a point of accuracy. The build was about 60 lines of code.

    Industry observers note that openRouter's auto model routing works through its Auto Router. You set the model to openrouter/auto, and a decision model picks a model and a reasoning effort for each request. You pay the standard rate of whichever model it selects, with no extra fee.

    Recent findings suggest that openClaw model routing is a primary model plus an ordered list of fallbacks. In the OpenClaw model routing configuration you set agents.defaults.model.primary and agents.defaults.model.fallbacks, and an agent can override the fallback list. When a model fails, OpenClaw first rotates auth profiles on the same provider, then moves to the next model on the list, as its model failover docs describe. That makes it fallback routing, not cost-based routing.

    An AI gateway simplifies model routing by putting every model behind one API, one set of keys, and one place for logs. Your app calls the gateway, and the routing rules live in config instead of code, so changing a model doesn't need a deploy.

    Sources indicate that mid-stream failover is when a router switches models after a streamed response has already started, because the first model failed partway through. It's the hardest kind of failover, because the user has already seen part of an answer. Many routers only fail over before the first token arrives and return an error after that, so check what your gateway does.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    GTA 6 players think they’ve found the real-life fursuit that inspired Chase, the fox-suited character you can save from the cops in a viral random encounter.

    Being a furry is illegal in GTA 6’s fictional state of Leonida. An in-game TV ad from the Anti-Furry Association urges residents to report suspected furry activity and warns tourists that hunting season is open. Dexerto previously covered the in-game ban and encounter.

    The ban plays out in a nighttime standoff, with police surrounding Chase under a helicopter spotlight. Players can give him a ride, lose the cops, and help him and another fursuited character reach the Furverts’ compound.

    Despite furries being illegal in GTA 6, you can actually save them if you wantA furry called Chase offers you $15,000 in cash or a custom SMG in exchange for helping them pic.twitter.com/SkZ21atE5r.

    Recent findings suggest that fans comparing Chase with fursuiter FoxiFelix zeroed in on the knees. Both suits have white shooting stars in roughly the same spot on each leg, with three stripes trailing from each star. The fox heads differ, and Felix spotted another resemblance after watching the encounter on YouTube, saying the tails looked alike.

    Felix also said Chase meowing in the van reminded them of something they do themselves.

    According to recent reports, I've just watched the encounter on YouTube and holy fuck so much is the same it's wild haha. Even the tail is the heccin same ❤️ The fact that chase starts meowing in the van fucking sent me as THATS LITERALLY WHAT I DO 😅.

    Sources indicate that YCHsuits, one of the makers Felix credits for their suit, also weighed in. The maker remarked Rockstar used one of its designs for the furry storyline and added that someone else made the fursuit’s head.

    I already did – the basis is off of a suit I made back in 2020 x3 (barring the head).

    It has been revealed that another fursuiter, Chase the Fox, remarked their DMs blew up after people connected them to the character. The two share a name and wear fox suits, while the shooting-star markings are the detail fans keep pointing to in the FoxiFelix comparison.

    My DMs are exploding right now because apparently I'M the furry in GTA VI and I was honestly not prepared to hear that when I woke up today 😭 pic.twitter.com/nTl3KkPvwq.

    Rockstar has yet to publicly confirm what inspired Chase’s design.

    #93318. Fitbit Edge after 30 days: Life in the middle lane [Video]

    📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1470 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 9to5google ↗ Open Full Page

    Fitbit Edge after 30 days: Life in the middle lane [Video]

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1470 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5google

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The biggest compliment you can pay Google at the moment is that alongside the Pixel Watch, recent Fitbit releases have been a huge return to form – the Fitbit Edge included.
    • I need to nail my colors to the mast; I’m a Fitbit Air fanboy.
    • The Fitbit Edge worried me at first because it comes with a screen, which is something I realized isn’t that important to me day-to-day.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The biggest compliment you can pay Google at the moment is that alongside the Pixel Watch, recent Fitbit releases have been a huge return to form – the Fitbit Edge included.

    I need to nail my colors to the mast; I’m a Fitbit Air fanboy. I’ve talked about it multiple times on the Pixelated podcast, here on the site, and it made me switch away from the Pixel Watch 5 because of how easily it fit into my existence without insisting on itself.

    The Fitbit Edge worried me at first because it comes with a screen, which is something I realized isn’t that important to me day-to-day. After 30 days of wear, I’m conflicted because maybe I was too hasty to ditch a display on my wrist.

    Industry observers note that the design is somewhat in a halfway house because it feels like it’s trying to be both a classic Fitbit while integrating some of the Pixel Watch features we know and love. Initially, I loved it, but it has become something that isn’t quite enough in either direction to suit my own tastes.

    Industry observers note that my love for the simplicity of the Fitbit Air has colored how I feel, but the Edge has an excellent core design. The display bezels remind me heavily of the original Pixel Watch; yes, they’re there, but you only notice them when the light catches the frame edge.

    After a month of daily wear, the display has lost a bit of its luster. The oleophobic coating is just about holding up, but now we’re into the cooler months; it’ll be put through a barrage of jacket cuffs and hoodie sleeves. This is one of the only durability concerns I have had so far.

    Sources indicate that despite that admittedly minor concern, the Fitbit Edge is not something you need to baby. I’ve bashed it with weights, caught my wrist on zips (zippers for you, my American friends), and bashed it around with reckless abandon. It’s solid and hasn’t picked up as much as a single scuff. I don’t care too much if a fitness tracker gets a beating, whereas I would be more concerned about damaging my Pixel Watch.

    Recent findings suggest that if you come in wanting a smartwatch-like experience from the Fitbit Edge, I think you’ll instantly be frustrated by the UI. It can feel cramped when you see notifications, and the large bezels don’t help all that much, but Google has well optimized almost all of the key sections outside of this.

    Sources indicate that tiles are very well implemented; they’re just a smaller, squatter take on the Pixel Watch tile system, and it’s one of the best things about the Fitbit Edge interface. It’s also really snappy, which is something that isn’t the case with cheaper fitness trackers such as this. I’m constantly checking the weather or using the Google Health tile, but I have loved the quick access complication on the default watch face.

    I tried a few of the other designs over the past 30 days; a lot of them are great. The default has become my favorite. It’s information-dense without being too overloaded. Tapping the complications takes you to the exact data point. I genuinely love how fuss-free an experience it is, save for a few minor complaints.

    Industry observers note that we could criticize the accuracy of the data or the lack of tracking for certain types of workouts, but I think that misses the point of the Fitbit Edge. It’s a simple tracker with a screen, and the fact that you get even basic ECG on a device of this size is impressive.

    Industry observers note that I truly have worn the Edge daily for a full month, and while the bands are comfortable, I have found that they cause me to get a rash on the underside of my left wrist just under the palm. It’s actively stopping me from wearing it all the time now. I hope that the new connector doesn’t slow down third-party development for bands, because I’m desperate for a fabric band to alleviate this issue.

    This is exacerbated when the rubber band gets wet or sweaty. If you have sensitive skin, you might have the same problem as I have. Using some moisturizer has helped, but it is something I wasn’t prepared to suffer with before the Fitbit Edge turned up. I get that this is likely a “me” problem, but I wanted to note it.

    Sources indicate that when the screen gets wet or moist, it can bug out quite a lot. Taps don’t register properly, and a few water droplets can activate all the menus and submenus. Luckily, it won’t force your phone to place a call or anything like that, but the water protection mode is a must. I have kept it on extensively.

    Swimmers will probably get super frustrated; heck, I was on a rainy day as the screen kept bugging out. Overall, though, I have enjoyed the fitness tracking. Unlike on the Fitbit Air, it is nice to have a screen to start a workout rather than head over to my phone. That said, the experience is the same as on your phone, but scaled down to fit the watch face.

    I dislike that you don’t get a phone notification to show the current workout progress by default, like the Fitbit Air. I had become accustomed to that. Luckily, you can enable it in the Google Health settings. I like having this as I forget to stop workouts so often without a prompt to hit “stop.”.

    Sources indicate that with audio playback, you’re also getting the partial benefits of watch-phone controls, but it’s a two-step process unlike on Pixel Watch. You either have to go to the “Media” app or have the tile active and navigate to it to access play/pause and all your other streaming app controls. I tend not to bother using these as it’s finicky.

    It has been revealed that this had me thinking about NFC. I think a lot of people would have liked NFC for Google Wallet on the Fitbit Edge, but I think having to enter a PIN on such a small screen would really have been a nightmare. I’ve made wireless payments with my watch less than five times, as it’s just easier to use my phone rather than contort my wrist to a wireless payment terminal. I figure this was something that was thought about and makes a lot of sense given the constraints.

    One of my other complaints is that the DND and Bedtime modes from my account haven’t synced or at least don’t appear to sync. Unless I’m mistaken, you need to activate these settings manually every time, which has been super annoying when in bed, as a flick of your wrist can blind you in a dark room. I figure this is something that can be fixed with an patch, so here’s hoping.

    I’ve been super impressed with the battery life. A week is easily attainable for me with up to three gym visits per week, so I’ve charged 5 times in a month. That, to me, is excellent. I picked up a cheap charging dock, as the Edge uses the same charger for the Fitbit Air, so I figured why not.

    It’s not the best-looking dock, but I quite like how it airs off my Edge so it’s not as stinky after gym sessions – as I wipe with an alcohol pad and clean as regularly as possible.

    It has been revealed that the experience is fine; it’s almost a third of the price of the Pixel Watch and lacks a few features due to the various compromises – compromises I can deal with, as smartwatches have become information overload for me over time, and I like that the app selection is ultra-refined. At no point does the Fitbit Edge give you information overload.

    According to recent reports, coming from a Charge 6 or an older Fitbit, this is an amazing replacement. It’s the upcoming “default” fitness tracker for people who want all the hallmarks of what makes a great Fitbit.

    According to recent reports, there is just enough. Nothing more, nothing less. To me, this feels like the perfect middle ground for a lot of people. You want something simple, touchscreen-enabled, and that doesn’t get in the way. As impressed as I have been with the Edge, though, I’ve loved a fuss-free tech accessory so much recently that I’ll probably go back to the Fitbit Air.

    #93317. Lawyer’s $9,450 private AI server with 12 used Nvidia V100s now runs every DeepSeek V4.1 Flash expert

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (867 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Tomshardware ↗ Open Full Page

    Lawyer’s $9,450 private AI server with 12 used Nvidia V100s now runs every DeepSeek V4.1 Flash expert

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (867 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that A lawyer has upped the ante by upgrading his private AI server from eight to 12 used Nvidia V100s, which can run every DeepSeek V4.1 Flash expert at 4-bit NVFP4.
    • It has been revealed that some of the best movie franchises come in threes, and Nick Mermiges seems determined to match that, taking his original setup — which he previously upgraded with more memory and other fixes — and expanding it for fuller precision, after a previous upgrade got him most of the way there.
    • In a recent development, the original eight 32GB cards could manage 254 GiB, but the experts for the chosen model, with Nvidia’s NVFP4 release, need 278.9 GiB.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that A lawyer has upped the ante by upgrading his private AI server from eight to 12 used Nvidia V100s, which can run every DeepSeek V4.1 Flash expert at 4-bit NVFP4. Performance can reach up to 184 tokens per second for code, and long documents start answering in about half the time as before. He claims it can outrun published DGX Spark stacks at decoding a single request, for half the price of three units, based on the $9,450 he paid.

    It has been revealed that some of the best movie franchises come in threes, and Nick Mermiges seems determined to match that, taking his original setup — which he previously upgraded with more memory and other fixes — and expanding it for fuller precision, after a previous upgrade got him most of the way there. The newest upgrade, this time, involves a third board of V100s, for a total of 12 with four per board. There may be a method to his madness.

    In a recent development, the original eight 32GB cards could manage 254 GiB, but the experts for the chosen model, with Nvidia’s NVFP4 release, need 278.9 GiB. His previous workaround was to have every expert on the cards at 2-bit precision, with the most-used, 5,949 or about 38.7%, swapped to NVFP4 until the cards were full. Now, all 15,360 experts can live on the cards in their full glory, as he intended, with “none compressed further,” according to his GitHub repo. In a longer write-up on his site, he notes the expert values “equal the ones in DeepSeek’s own release,” although other parts of the model use compact forms.

    A keen observer will notice a limitation of the V100s, which he spells out: the V100 has no FP4 or FP8 tensor cores. Every NVFP4 number has to be unpacked in software, first, and into half precision. The compact experts still pay off “because the cards read fewer bytes, not because they compute faster.” This helps explain why a card from 2018 can run a format from the Blackwell era.

    According to recent reports, the model’s layers are, again, divided among the boards, this time with 0–13, 14–27, and 28–39, and each board’s section is split across its own four cards. The cards on a board share Nvidia’s fast link, or NVLink, and the hand-offs between boards cross over the host’s PCIe through two separate PCIe switches. The first two boards share a PEX88096 switch, so their hand-off stays inside it, but the third board is behind a separate PLX 8749, so the second hand-off also has to cross the host’s PCIe bridges, which adds latency.

    All this trouble is worth it, though, as with different settings — each card’s power cap raised from 150 W to 175 W and its clock cap lowered from 1,522 MHz to 1,452 MHz — there are noticeable improvements to performance as well as precision.

    Industry observers note that his measurements show the first code token, with 256K context, at 58 seconds, almost twice as fast as the 108.4 seconds after his previous upgrade. Prompt reading is at “about 4,500 tokens a second” past 32K, which is more than twice the roughly 2,200 tokens a second of his first build, though the higher power cap likely accounts for some of that. Code decode, meanwhile, is 23% faster at 1K, but shows no real gains at 32K and up, so the real gain is a reduced wait for the first token.

    Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

    There was some eagerness to get more out of the system by pushing each card to 200 W for a day, but “the host tripped once under four long chats at once,” implying the power draw was perhaps too much. He also worked to optimize the setup as much as possible, but four optimizations — a conversation store that saves to disk, a leaner hand-off between sections, tighter expert packing, and exact four-card-sum arithmetic — had to be turned off due to missing their targets.

    According to recent reports, another common technique is to run multiple requests at once, usually netting a speed improvement. In this case, three requests at 128K got about 360 tokens per second in total on code and 213 on legal. That mentioned, “this is not a batched-decode engine; more requests than sections gain little.”.

    According to recent reports, however, that might be next on the docket, as he looks to study batched decoding, “the one thing the Sparks have that I want,” he wrote on Reddit. Beyond that, there are plans to turn on the conversation store so a matter’s documents can survive a restart. While he acknowledges that the numbers do not establish “answer quality in use,” the setup has been his default DeepSeek machine since Monday, and he claims the model is the first one “that works like Opus 4.6” for him.
