    #93315. Vivo X500 Pro camera review: Battle of the small(er) phones vs Pixel 11 Pro

    📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (871 w)
    📖 Baca
    Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 9to5google ↗ Open Full Page

    Vivo X500 Pro camera review: Battle of the small(er) phones vs Pixel 11 Pro

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (871 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5google

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The compact Vivo X500 Pro has some camera downgrades compared to the Pro Max, so are you better off saving money and getting the base Vivo X500 instead?
    • Industry observers note that over the past few years, Vivo has made a name for itself as the camera powerhouse smartphone company.
    • Industry observers note that the answer is mostly yes.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The compact Vivo X500 Pro has some camera downgrades compared to the Pro Max, so are you better off saving money and getting the base Vivo X500 instead?

    Industry observers note that over the past few years, Vivo has made a name for itself as the camera powerhouse smartphone company. The first time I used a Vivo X100 Pro blew my mind in a way smartphone cameras hadn’t for a few years, but does the company’s 4th iteration — yes, Vivo skipped the X400 — of the X series still impress?

    Industry observers note that the answer is mostly yes. The Vivo X500 series includes five models: the base X500, the X500 Pro, and the X500 Pro Max. Unlike some other phones, all three of these models feature different camera hardware that takes advantage of the physical size differences. The X500 Pro Max’s hardware is the best of the bunch, but that phone is substantially larger and heavier as a result.

    So I’m comparing the more reasonably sized models to see which semi-compact Vivo phone you should consider this year. I tossed the Google Pixel 11 Pro into the comparison since Google also offers a compact flagship camera phone.

    Sources indicate that most camera specs between these phones are surprisingly comparable, so the differences you’re about to see are largely caused by some pretty massive differences in processing. I already covered Vivo’s wild latest AI camera mode, so let’s go for something a little closer to normal smartphone camera use: a day at the Biltmore.

    Recent findings suggest that perhaps the biggest difference between these phones is Vivo’s pursuit of “perfection,” while Google seems to embrace a more “natural” look. At 10x and 5x, the photos from both Vivo phones are essentially noise-free, have clear sharpening applied to them, and are generally quite vibrant. Despite having similar specs, the Vivo X500 Pro’s more advanced Sony LYT telephoto sensor pulls out more detail.

    Google’s images are notably softer, although not in a low-resolution sort of way. They look more like they’re taken from a standard camera rather than a smartphone, which some people may prefer. While telephoto image quality between the Vivo X500 Pro and Google Pixel 11 Pro is mostly down to preference, Google’s phone is substantially faster while taking the actual photo. In all of the darker shots, the Pixel 11 Pro took the picture instantly. Both Vivo X500 models took a 2-3 second exposure shot, making me stand there for longer than I’m used to.

    Ultrawide performance is where I feel we see the largest gap between these phones. Both the Vivo X500 and X500 Pro cameras offer bright, well-balanced shots that are vibrant but not unrealistic. The light sources in the room emit a lovely warm glow, yet the bulbs themselves aren’t overblown. The X500 Pro’s slightly warmer image across all three scenarios looks best to me.

    It has been revealed that the Pixel 11 Pro’s ultrawide images are often underexposed and lacking in dynamic range. The staircase shot exhibits this problem the most. This can come off as natural in some scenarios, as modern smartphone photography is notorious for brightening dark areas too much, but too often the Pixel 11 Pro’s ultrawide shots just feel unnaturally dark.

    The main camera is much more balanced, although it’s fun to push these phones to find their weaknesses. One of the best examples of differing priorities is in the wreath shot, which was quite dark in real life thanks to the bright sunlight outside. The Pixel 11 Pro valiantly tried to brighten up the shadows so you could actually see the wreath (since it’s clearly the subject), causing the rest of the scene to look forcefully bright.

    Sources indicate that the same matter cropped up in the image of the wine rack, where both Vivo phones captured a nicer-looking shot. The image of the trellis walkway is a tie, but the photo of my ridiculous bowl of ice cream looks best on the Vivo X500 Pro, once again.

    Portrait mode is where I think the Vivo X500 Pro is the clear loser, but it’s not for any of the reasons in the other categories above. Rather, the X500 Pro seems to have some weird warping happening in the bokeh processing that’s not present on the base Vivo X500. This is in both front-facing and rear camera portrait shots, so it’s not a lens concern or some weird setting.

    Google cleaned up its portrait shots so much this year that it’s borderline ridiculous. Pixels had the worst portrait mode for years, but this year’s overhaul of the portrait algorithm made all the difference in the world.

    Overall, the Vivo X500 series is another solid release for Vivo, and while neither the base nor Pro models offer the same top-tier camera specs as the Pro Max model, it’s clear Vivo pulled off something great. The Vivo X500 Pro retails for €1,399 in the EU, while the base X500 global model is a little harder to find, but should be quite a bit cheaper if you can get your hands on it.

    Google Play is introducing latest adaptive app and game quality requirements next year to elevate the Android foldable experience.

    Starting April 2027, the Play Store will require developers to meet Tier 3 of the Android adaptive app quality guidelines for foldables.

    Recent findings suggest that referred to as “Adaptive ready” or “basic” support, Tier 3 requires apps not to use letterboxing (or other compatibility modes) and to fill the entire screen. During rotation, resizing, and folding/unfolding, apps must preserve scroll position, text input, and media playback. Apps must also support multi-window environments.

    Apps that do not meet this quality bar will no longer be able to publish or update on Google Play, and may have reduced visibility on the store.

    At the same time, Google Play will require foldable device screenshots for app listings: “Providing foldable screenshots by April 2027 will become a standard submission requirement when publishing upcoming apps or updating your store listing.”.

    Curious to see whether the requirements will actually be as strict as they make them seem (on paper).

    If so, then also Google will have a ton of work to do to modernise all of their apps.

    By August 2027, newly introduced and updated apps will be required to target Android 17 (API level 37).

    Over time, this “quality framework will progressively expand to incorporate Tier 2 and Tier 1 standards across foldables, tablets, Googlebooks, and Android XR.”.

    Apps that meet Tier 2 (better) or Tier 1 (best) will get “premier store badging, editorial spotlighting, and enhanced merchandising across Google Play as the platform bar elevates.”.

    On the gaming front, titles will need to add foldable screenshots to listings by April 2027, while Tier 3 large screen quality guidelines go into effect in August 2027.

    Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

    In a recent development, weekly. Free. One click to leave.

    In a recent development, 7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

    According to recent reports, elementor made your site easy to build. It may also be making it slow. Here's how to move a site onto the Block Editor without breaking URLs, losing content or dropping out of Google.

    Recent findings suggest that page builders solved a real problem. Before the Block Editor matured, they were the easiest way to give clients drag-and-drop layouts. Many of those sites are still running today, and a lot of them are slow on phones.

    Industry observers note that the data backs that up. According to the HTTP Archive Core Web Vitals Technology Report for June 2026, 36.8% of Elementor sites pass Core Web Vitals on mobile. Sites built with the Block Editor pass 53.0% of the time. That's correlation, not proof, since hosting and setup matter too. But in my experience, it matches what happens when you remove the builder from a slow site.

    In a recent development, my reason for migrating sites off Elementor is simple: **page builders make websites heavy. **Having stated that, Elementor has improved a lot. Its performance settings, Flexbox Containers, and asset-loading options cut much of the bloat, and a carefully tuned Elementor site can pass Core Web Vitals. But tuning only goes so far. You’re still shipping the builder’s framework, wrapper markup and scripts, and every plugin or Elementor revision is a chance for the speed to slip again.

    For small business sites that don’t need drag-and-drop editing, rebuilding the same design on the WordPress Block Editor (Gutenberg) removes that weight at the source, without changing what the client sees.

    Sources indicate that this guide follows the order I use. It assumes you're comfortable with WordPress admin, WP-CLI and a staging site. If you need to set those up first, SitePoint's guide to the ultimate WordPress development environment covers the tooling.

    Recent findings suggest that not every Elementor site needs to move. Migration makes sense when:.

    It's harder to justify when the site leans on Elementor Pro features you'd need to replace, such as complex popups, dynamic loops or WooCommerce templates. Those can all be rebuilt, but the job gets bigger fast.

    According to recent reports, you can't prove a migration worked without "before" numbers. Capture these on the live site first.

    According to recent reports, crawl the site with a tool such as Screaming Frog, and export every indexable URL with its title, meta description, H1 and canonical tag. You can also pull published pages and posts with WP-CLI:.

    Run Google PageSpeed Insights, which uses Lighthouse for its lab scores, on the homepage and two or three key templates. Save the mobile lab scores and, if the site has enough traffic, the field data from real consumers.

    Export the last three months of pages and queries from Google Search Console. That's what you'll compare against after launch.

    According to recent reports, elementor stores each page's layout as JSON in the elementordata post meta field, and marks builder pages with elementoredit_mode. This command lists every page that uses the builder:.

    Then list everything else Elementor controls, which is easy to miss:.

    It has been revealed that on the small business sites I've migrated, the inventory usually turns up more than the owner expects. The pages are the easy part. The surprises are saved templates nobody remembers creating, a popup still running on every page, add-on widgets from plugins that were installed once and forgotten, and contact forms that live inside Elementor Pro rather than a form plugin. Finding those before the rebuild saves a broken launch.

    It has been revealed that work on a staging copy. Install a block theme, such as Twenty Twenty-Five or a lightweight starter theme, and move the Elementor global styles into theme.json. That way colors, fonts and spacing are defined once, instead of in every widget.

    Copy the hex values and font names from Elementor's Site Settings so the fresh site matches the old one. Rebuild the header and footer as template parts in the Site Editor. If you'd rather write a theme yourself, SitePoint's series on building a WordPress theme from scratch covers the basics.

    Recent findings suggest that most Elementor sites repeat the same few sections: a hero, a services grid, testimonials and a call to action. Build each one once as a block pattern, then reuse it on every page. Patterns are plain block markup, so you don't need React to write them, whatever you may have heard about React and WordPress development.

    In a block theme, any PHP file in the /patterns folder with a header comment is registered automatically:.

    For page content, there's a useful shortcut. Elementor saves a plain HTML copy of each page into post_content. Open a page in the Block Editor, and the old content usually appears in a Classic block. Choose Convert to blocks, then delete the leftovers and rebuild the layout with your patterns. It keeps the copy and images, so you only redo the design.

    The difference shows up in the page source. Here's typical front-end markup for a single heading on an Elementor page, using the older section and column layout:.

    And the same heading as a block:.

    Newer Elementor versions with Flexbox containers and the optimized markup settings trim some of those wrappers, but most older sites still carry all of them. Multiply that by every element on every page, and the weight adds up.

    According to recent reports, to speed up this step, I built a free Elementor to Gutenberg converter. Paste in a page's elementordata JSON from Step 2, and it returns block markup you can paste into the Block Editor's code editor. It handles headings, text, images, buttons, spacers, dividers and column layouts, and lists anything it can't convert, such as forms and popups, for you to rebuild by hand. It runs entirely in your browser, so the page data never leaves your computer.

    Industry observers note that the code is rarely what holds a migration up. Content is. Once clients see their site being rebuilt, many decide it's time to rewrite their pages too, and the project ends up waiting on copywriters and approvals. My fix is to separate the two: migrate the existing content as it is, launch, then patch the copy afterwards. That keeps the speed and SEO gains on schedule, and it means any ranking change can be traced to either the migration or the latest copy, not both at once.

    This is the step that decides whether rankings hold.

    To spot-check a redirect or a status code from the command line:.

    Industry observers note that when staging matches the live site, deploy it. Then:.

    Sources indicate that leave the old elementordata meta in place for a few weeks, in case you need to roll back. Once you're confident, take a backup and remove it to shrink the database.

    Run PageSpeed Insights again straight away for lab scores. Field data takes longer: the Chrome UX Report uses a rolling 28-day window, so give it a month before judging real-user results. Compare Search Console clicks for the same period before and after launch.

    In my migrations, the biggest change is usually page weight and loading time, because the builder's CSS, JavaScript and wrapper markup are gone. What doesn't always improve is server response time. If the site is on slow shared hosting, the first byte still arrives late, and that needs a hosting fix, not a rebuild. Search traffic should hold steady if the URLs and metadata were protected. If it drops, the Step 5 crawl comparison is the first place to look.

    Moving off Elementor isn't a one-click job, but it isn't a full redesign either. Record a baseline, inventory what the builder controls, rebuild with patterns, and protect every URL. Most of the speed gain comes from removing code the site never needed. For what to tackle after that, see these practical web performance techniques. Most of the risk comes from rushing the SEO checks. Done carefully, the client gets the same site, a faster one, and an editor that comes with WordPress itself.

    Some GTA 6 players have already found a new favorite in Vicki, a goth bartender they meet just one chapter after Mandy.

    Sources indicate that vicki works at Delights, a strip club in Port Gellhorn, and lives in Room 10 at the Starlet Motel. Lucia first meets her there in “Girls’ Trip” while looking for painkillers for Jason. When the pills Vicki sells her turn out to be over-the-counter medicine, the two head into town to track down Vicki’s dealer.

    Industry observers note that it took just one scene in Chapter 1 for Mandy to win over players. She talks Jason into fixing her sink while he’s out collecting money for Brian. The object he pulls from the pipe looks like a severed finger, which led to the theory that Mandy might be a serial killer.

    When X user @AerisTreat posted about Vicki on November 20, players in the replies started picking sides.

    Oooh shit PT.2 pic.twitter.com/JroGxh3CS2.

    “Mandy is so overrated, Vicki is where it’s at,” one player wrote. Another called GTA 6 “Game of the year just for her,” while a third wished the game had a friendship mechanic for side characters so Vicki and Lucia could be best friends.

    Industry observers note that one player said they’d already been to Delights and hadn’t seen Vicki behind the bar. AerisTreat told them to look for her on the second story visit to the club, during “Afternoon Delight.”.

    Sources indicate that the mission opens up after “Coffee Break” in Chapter 2, when Vicki calls Jason and Lucia with a plan to rob her boss, Frankie. It’s ladies’ night when they arrive, and if players agree to help when Frankie asks whether Jason can dance, Jason takes the stage while Lucia goes after the safe.
